speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: APPROVAL OF INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT OPENED FOR SIGNATURE AT WASHINGTON, MARCH 6, 1948
speechtext:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve the international wheat agreement opened for signature at Washington on March 6, 1948, and that this house do approve the same.

International Wheat Agreement
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving this resolution I am asking the house to approve Canada's participation in the international wheat agreement which was opened for signature at Washington on March 6, 1948, and signed on behalf of thirty-six countries, including Canada. No additional legislation is required to implement this agreement so long as the present authority remains under the Canadian Wheat Board Act or under the Export and Import Permits Act.
Formal acceptance of this agreement is required by July 1 of each of the countries whose legislative bodies have been in session since the agreement was signed. For example, I understand that the agreement is now before the United States senate for ratification as a treaty, in order that the United States government may give its formal acceptance by July 1, and in order that the agreement may become operative commencing with the new crop year on the first of August.
I think that members will be interested in hearing something of the background leading up to this agreement. I need not dwell on the pre-war period, or on the international agreements and proposals of those days, beyond pointing out that the terms of those earlier agreements were quite different from the terms of the agreement we have before us for approval today. The old idea was to influence prices indirectly by regulating or restricting supplies. The present agreement is a multilateral contract covering the sale of wheat. It is a price and quantity agreement drawn up between three exporting countries and thirty-three importing countries, and does not in any way affect additional wheat transactions, either between member countries or with non-member countries once the transactions provided in the agreement are met.
Since the end of the war, this government has consistently supported the objective of obtaining a measure of stability in international wheat prices. With the hearty support of our wheat producers' organizations we instructed our officials to further these views with other governments, both through the international wheat council and through the food and agriculture organization.
By the spring of 1946 it was apparent that an international agreement on wheat prices could not be reached in time to affect the 1946-47 crop year, and in lieu thereof Canada concluded a bilateral contract with its principal wheat customer, the United Kingdom. In the meantime, negotiations toward an international wheat agreement were continued, one conference being held in London in the spring of 1947, at which agreement was almost
reached, and the second conference being held in Washington early this year, at which the present agreement was concluded.
The agreement involves the annual sale of 500 million bushels of wheat over a period of the next five crop years, of which Canada's share is 230 million bushels. This figure represents our normal export surplus from crops grown on our existing acreage. The agreement provides for a range of prices all based on No. 1 northern wheat, in store Fort William-Port Arthur, with a uniform ceiling of $2 over the five-year period and floors commencing with $1.50 in the first year and declining by ten cents per year until the floor of $1.10 is reached in the fifth crop year. Each of the importing countries is assigned a share of the total 500 million bushels, and they have the right to buy and the exporting countries have an obligation to sell these quantities at the ceiling prices. Conversely, the exporting countries have a right to sell and the importing countries an obligation to buy these same quantities at the floor prices. In brief, this means that the importing countries have an assurance of supplies at not more than ceiling prices, and the exporting countries have the assurance of a market at not less than floor prices to the extent of the agreement quantities.
As I mentioned before, the agreement in no way affects wheat purchases by the memberimporting countries in excess of their commitments under the agreement from any source whatever, nor does it affect the sales of the member-exporting countries if they have wheat for sale in excess of their commitments. The 500 million bushels in the agreement by no means exhausts the current volume of the world wheat trade, which is running upwards of 850 million bushels per year.
It has been frequently mentioned that Argentina and Russia are not parties to this agreement. They were given every opportunity to join, but they declined. Because the agreement is in the form of a sales contract, its operation and the interests of its member countries are not affected by the absence of these two countries. Under surplus conditions, it can be assumed that Argentina and Russia will offer their wheat below the floor prices set out in the agreement. Canada, Australia and the United States, however, have the protection of floor prices on their normal export surpluses, and are free to meet Argentine and Russian competition on any additional quantities they may desire to sell. On the other hand, should the importing countries produce more of their own Wheat, their imports will be maintained from Canada, Australia and the United States, while diminishing from other sources.
International Wheat Agreement

The international agreement does not limit our rights under the Canada-United Kingdom wheat agreement. The fixed price of $2 per bushel for the third year of that agreement will continue in force for the 1948-49 crop year on our sales under the contract to the United Kingdom. The price for the fourth year of the contract is to be negotiated under the terms of the contract before December 31 of this year.
The agreement is noncommittal on the issue of state versus private trading between the member countries. Under the same agreement the Canadian and Australian wheat boards will continue for the present to make wheat sales for their respective countries, while wheat sales from the United States will be made by the private trade. Flour exports from each of the three exporting countries are to continue under private trade. Because of the breadth of the price ranges there is ample room for the operation of markets within the limits of the price ranges. What the agreement accomplishes is to rule out the extreme situations beyond either end of the price range which have hitherto brought undesirable consequences in their wake and which have been the main source of resentment against the open market system as it has operated in the past.
Because of the variations in our crop yields and consequent uncertainty of supplies, it has been impossible for us to deal as a single exporter with a number of our other wheat customers on the same basis as we have been dealing with the United Kingdom for the past two years. By combining the resources of the three wheat exporting countries under an international agreement, it will be possible for us to deal with all our wheat customers alike in return for like obligations on their part, and on the same terms in which they are being dealt with by the United States and Australia, if the international wheat agreement is formally accepted by the countries concerned.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this wheat agreement is very much in the interests of Canada, and I recommend its acceptance.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: APPROVAL OF INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT OPENED FOR SIGNATURE AT WASHINGTON, MARCH 6, 1948
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution
before us asks us to approve a wheat agreement between three exporting countries and thirty-three importing countries. So far as the facts are concerned the minister's statement, I think, covers the situation very well. I do not propose to take up very much of the time of the house, but the situation does deserve some comment, even though the measure will no doubt pass the house unanimously.
No one in Canada, I think, would have any opposition to the objective of this agree-

ment. The difficulty in connection with w'heat in the past has been its wide fluctuations in price, due partly to widely differing volumes of production, and sometimes to international interference. Within a very few years the price of wheat has varied from 40 cents to $3.40 per bushel. When the price is $3.40 a bushel our wheat farmers are prosperous, while those who import wheat feel very differently about the price. When it is 40 cents a bushel, or anything approaching that figure, our wheat farmers go broke and our economy becomes disturbed. It is for this reason that for more than two decades efforts have been made to lessen these wide fluctuations in price, but for the most part, I am afraid, not with much success.
The objective, I say, of this measure is most laudable. But the plan now before us is in my judgment inadequate and unfinished, and far from being a perfect instrument to meet the situation. The results, therefore, from its passage are likely to be disappointing to Canadian producers if they are expecting large results from this measure in its present form.
The minister has referred to the background leading up to the present situation. I should like also to refer to that background. As the minister stated, this is not the first wheat agreement into which Canada has entered, and it is not the first wheat agreement into which this government has entered. The experience of this government in connection with international wheat agreements has not been such as to offer much promise in the way of good results. Nevertheless, that is no argument against our continuing to try to get an instrument that will get us the results we want.
What have been the experiences of recent years? In 1942 the Canadian government entered into a temporary wheat agreement seeking to achieve some price stability when the war was over. One provision of that agreement was that if a final agreement as to price had not been completed by six months after the end of hostilities, the price charged for export wheat would be the amount received per bushel by the largest exporter for the last bulk shipment to the chief importer. It turned out that that was a shipment from Canada to the United Kingdom and the price was $1.55 a bushel. This agreement of 1942 was agreed to by several different nations, but what happened? The Canadian government alone adhered to that agreement, and no other party to the agreement did. The result was that other nations sold their wheat at much higher prices, and

International Wheat Agreement
Canada and Canadian farmers thereby lost scores of million of dollars. There were no doubt other reasons why that particular price was accepted by the Canadian government, but that agreement to which Canada alone adhered was the initiation of this price of $1.55 a bushel.
Then in the year 1946 this government entered into another international wheat agreement called the United Kingdom-Canada agreement, commonly known as the British wheat agreement. It was an agreement between those two countries providing for the sale by Canada of four crops of wheat, or the huge volume of 600 million bushels, at a price starting at $1.55 a bushel and subject during the four-year period to adjustment, but never to go below, I think, $1 a bushel. No other nation followed that policy. Every other nation sold its wheat for what it could get, and many of them got in different years twice as much, and some of them nearly three times as much, for certain sales of wheat as Canada got. Yet Canada sold at $1.55 and let her farmers take the loss.
Now we come to the present agreement of which the minister has spoken. Three exporting countries, Canada, the United States and Australia, undertake to deliver 500 million bushels of wheat per year to thirty-three importing countries under certain conditions with respect to price and amounts.
My first observation with respect to this agreement is that the Argentine is not in it. There was an earlier wheat agreement entered into in 1933, not only Canada, the United States and Australia were in that agreement, but the Argentine was in it too, and certain of the Danubian countries. That agreement of 1933 collapsed. Why? It collapsed, according to report, because the Argentine broke the terms of the agreement. Well, if the Argentine's withdrawal from that agreement, caused its collapse, what prospect is there of an agreement with the Argentine not in it at all? Not only is the Argentine not in it, but as the minister pointed out, the Danubian countries are not in it, and Russia is not in it. I am not aware that Russia was ever in any of those agreements, but certainly the Danubian countries and the Argentine were.
Let me refer now for a moment to the 1933 agreement, which was made before the present government came into power. The discussions regarding it started in 1929, almost twenty years ago. The agreement itself was consummated in 1933. The discussions arose at that time not because conditions were similar to those of today, but surpluses were depressing prices. Prices were low; the producers were concerned, and even purchasers in Europe were concerned. Because of those low prices, certain governments over in Europe, which used to import large amounts of our wheat, had put tariffs against our products until in certain of these western European countries they were paying tw7o or three times as much to their own growers to produce wheat as they needed to pay to Canada to get our wheat.
It was under these circumstances that these discussions took place. If my memory serves me correctly, five groups of exporting countries, the chief exporting countries of the world, entered into an arrangement with about tweny-five others which I might call importing countries. It might be more correct to say that the surplus-producing countries entered into an agreement with the deficit-producing countries, the countries that did not produce enough of this commodity to feed their own people.
Let me refer now to this immediate agreement. We are told that Australia has approved of this agreement, subject to the United States approval later on. I do not know whether Australia gave its approval subject to Canadian approval also, but probably that is so. Of the three exporting countries in it, only one has given it qualified approval.
With respect to the United States-now probably the most important member in this agreement-because if that country does not come into it, it will never be consummated- the matter is before the senate committee of the United States. Reports would indicate that the senate committee is not likely to give a favourable decision on the matter in time for it to be approved before July 1. I think that is the date the minister gave.

If it should not be approved by the United States within the next ten days, it will not go into effect for the present crop year.
What are the points we should examine in an important agreement such as this in order to arrive at a wise decision as to our attitude with respect to it? I suggest there are three. First of all there is the question of the price to be received by the exporting countries, and to be paid by the importing countries. The second important point is the amount to be delivered by the exporting countries and to be taken by the importing countries. The third, of course, is the prospect of its success or failure.
International Wheat Agreement

Let us look for a moment at the question of prices. We are told that during the life of this agreement the maximum price of wheat will be $2 a bushel, and that it may be as low as $1.10 a bushel. We are talking about selling one of Canada's greatest export commodities over a long period of future years at a price between $2 and SI.10 a bushel at a time when the actual price of wheat is much higher than the highest of these figures.
In the year 1946 we entered into an agreement to sell wheat at $1.55 a bushel. In one year it got up as high as $2 a bushel. In the first year of that agreement we found that the average price of wheat which was not locked up in this agreement was $2.44. In the second year of the agreement the average price of wheat not locked up in the agreement was around S3 a bushel, and we are now undertaking to tie this nation to the acceptance of a price between $2 and $1.10 a bushel when the price today is much higher than that.
In addition to that I want to draw attention to one other feature. Wheat at $2 a bushel today, with the prospect of going as low as $1.10, would be equivalent to what on the basis of pre-war values of money? Today we have a 60-cent or a 63-cent or a 65-cent dollar, or whatever it is. On the basis of prewar prices this would mean a maximum of $1.20 or $1.25 and a minimum of 66 or 70 cents. I ask hon. members, if we had been entering into an arrangement such as this prior to the war would we have agreed to a maximum price of say $1.25 and a minimum price of 66 to 70 cents a bushel? Would we have done it? I respectfully suggest that we would not. No one has any doubt as to that. The facts speak for themselves. In 1935, under a similar situation, this house approved of a policy of paying not 66 cents to 70 cents as a minimum, but paying 87i cents a bushel as an initial price. That was the price decided upon when there was a surplus burdening the market and the dollar was worth one hundred cents. At that time we said we should not sell our wheat at less than 87^- cents a bushel. If we translate the present inflationary figures to pre-war values we would be agreeing to sell our wheat at a price of somewhere between $1.25 and 70 cents a bushel. That would not have been high enough.
The agreement sets out also that Canada will provide 230 million bushels out of the total of 500 million bushels from the exporting countries. I do not think any reasonable man will criticize the share allotted to Canada. United States w'as allotted 185 million bushels, and Australia 85 million bushels, making a total of 500 million bushels. In the early agreement away back in 1933 the United States was mot the important exporting country that she

is today. She then occupied about fourth place. Today she is up to second place, and the action which that nation takes will largely determine whether an agreement of this kind will ever be consummated or whether, if it were consummated, it would be any good.
What is the chief weakness of the agreement? Some people say there is a joker in it, but I do not like that term. I do not think anyone is joking about this thing. I believe the government and the people of Canada want to find a way to lessen the wide fluctuation in prices of this commodity, which has such an important- bearing upon the stability of our economic life. But the weakness of the agreement is that some of the large exporting areas of the world are not in it. I refer to the Argentine, and to the Danubian countries, and to Soviet Russia. The chief weakness is that the Argentine is not in it.
There is another weakness in bringing this proposal forward at this time. I regard it as being in an unfinished state. I believe that any proposal that this nation is prepared to accept prices ranging from $2 down to $1.10 for wheat, suggests to the world that the price of wheat will go down, and go down pretty far and maybe pretty fast. And I am not one who believes that it is inevitable that prices will go down like that.
If the world wants this commodity it can have it, provided it is prepared >to pay the producers enough to grow it; and if it is not prepared to do that, a lesser supply will be produced, and the price will be high. I am wondering if we are not bringing on ourselves the worst of two worlds, suggesting to others that the price will go down, without the assurance that this agreement will even be entered into or that it will be successful if it is entered into. In that respect it is a shortsighted procedure.
I can summarize our position briefly on this matter. We will not- stand in the way of any efforts to arrive at some international agreement to provide some insurance against surpluses depressing prices. We will not stand in the way of any endeavour to get an agreement that will prevent these wide fluctuations which play such havoc with the economies particularly of exporting nations. We must keep on in that effort.
My second point is this. In my judgment this measure is far from a finished product. There are not enough nations in it, and particularly not enough exporting nations. The fact that the Argentine is out makes it, I was going to say, impossible to expect success from it. The fact that Russia and the Danubian countries are out makes it difficult. I am not hopeful that Russia will ever be in it, but

International Wheat Agreement
certainly the Danubian countries were in it once, and it may be difficult to get them in again. With the United States now ten days from the final date of ratification, and there being considerable doubt whether that country will ratify it this year, the chances are very slim that the agreement will go into effect this year. That is not an argument now against our indicating that something of this kind is wanted. In the position in which I find myself, it does raise doubts of its immediate need' or its eventual success. It is moving in the right direction, but I am afraid its weaknesses are not very promising for its success.
The third objection in my judgment is that the prices agreed to under these inflated conditions are too low.
If producers in Canada are counting on this agreement, in its present unfinished state, to provide anything in the way of better conditions for them, I want to be on record as indicating that, in its present state, I do not think we can expect much advantage from it. Nevertheless I agree that we must continue in these efforts and hope to reach the time when, if not all the nations, at least enough nations will stand together to see that these wide price fluctuations, which we cannot prevent unless we do stand together, are lessened.
These four or five points outline our general position on this resolution.

maintopic: APPROVAL OF INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT OPENED FOR SIGNATURE AT WASHINGTON, MARCH 6, 1948
speechtext:
I wish to speak on this subject because I think it is of greater concern than any other topic that has come before the house this session. I do so because, since I am both a producer and a consumer as well as a citizen of Canada, I think we recognize it as one of the great problems to produce and allocate food throughout the world, so that where we have a surplus it can be moved to places where food is needed.
Some of us have been greatly concerned about press reports which indicate that some of the signatories to the agreement may not ratify it before the close of the session. I speak particularly of the United States government, which has indicated that it may not sign the agreement before the close of the session of congress.
As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) has said, there have been attempts over the past fifteen years to reach some sort of international agreement between producer and consumer countries so as to allow for the intelligent flow of agricultural products to the countries that need them, and at the same time maintain a decent price to the producer.
In the western provinces we have often been forced to take our grain to the elevator and deliver it far below cost of production. I myself have delivered many thousands of bushels of oats, wheat and barley for less than it cost to produce them. As far as our own Canadian economy is concerned, we have seen in many parts of our province, as a result of low prices, that though the people did get large crops they were as hard up as other parts of the province where there was not a large production, the land being dried out.
We as producers rightfully ask that we be given cost of production for our commodity, but at the same time we wish to have these products go to the consumer at a fair price. In dealing with this whole intricate subject we have to realize that there are many phases of our economy which are interdependent in the production and distribution of foodstuffs. As I have indicated since coming to the house, one of the things we need is to put into practice the principle of the ever-normal granary. To do that we would need' to store in years of plenty at least 1,000 million bushels of wheat and other grains.
When there were short crops in the dominion we could live up to some of our international agreements, and that would be one deterrent to resistance on the part of importing countries to any sort of international agreement. However, in the past, under the open market system, we have found that when 'we had 200 million or 300 million bushels on hand, the product became a drug on the market, and prices were depressed.
In an effort to break down the negotiations for an international wheat agreement we have seen certain interests in Canada, namely the Winnipeg grain exchange, attempting to undermine those negotiations. A letter came to my office this morning from the Winnipeg grain exchange, a portion of which I intend to read to the house. The last paragraph, which makes reference to the agreement now under discussion, reads as follows:
For fifteen years a plan along those general lines has been actively promoted, but at every stage final action has failed to result because of disagreement among the nations or from nonobservance of the conditions laid down. It is a hard thing to get agreement among sovereign states and these states are bound to follow certain constitutional processes which take time. Another failure on this occasion will be but another evidence that governments are not suitable agencies for operating the details of a great commercial business like the wheat business.
If, Mr. Speaker, we are to get any basis of stability for our producers, the government must take a hand in this great operation in.
International Wheat Agreement

our country. It cannot be left to free enterprisers, or to the fluctuating markets of the grain exchange; rather we must enter into commodity agreements, preferably on a multilateral basis; whereby we can export to and import from other countries on a true value basis. It is just not intelligent to expect other countries to accept our wheat and other farm products unless we are ready to import from .those countries on a decent and equitable basis. If we try to export our commodities, as has been done in the past, and ask for a price structure which is out of line with the price we are prepared to pay for commodities from those countries, we cannot hope for any sort of workable international agreement.
I am also concerned because of what is taking place in the United States. I have in my hand a report which appears in this morning's Globe and Mail headed "U.S. wheat export will be returned to private hands." It says that the Commodity Credits Corporation are to put back in private hands the handling of wheat exports in the United States. The latter part of the article reads as follows:
A spokesman for the ECA-[DOT]
Which is the economic co-operation administration, in the United States, administering the Marshall plan for aid to Europe.
-says the move to put wheat exports back into private hands -would be completed within a month. The committee is agreed that the change should be made as soon as possible. The report of a fairly large wheat crop in the United States has encouraged1 the committee to act more quickly.
Here we have seen perhaps some success on the part of private individuals to thwart the efforts toward international agreements handled by governments. I think that if once more this international agreement is washed up, so to speak, we shall be back into the cutthroat competition we had prior to the last war; indeed, it will be a large factor in creating world conditions which tend toward another world war.
Among the people who want such agreements as this wheat agreement, we have the international federation of agricultural producers. At their second annual conference, held in Paris this year, they unanimously passed a resolution calling on all governments to sign the agreement, and the agreement now under discussion is the one referred to. That conference passed three resolutions which I intend to read to the house. They are as follows:
(a)	It is essential that effective machinery should be provided to deal with surpluses which may develop, to ensure that they are directed to the areas of the greatest need, and that such surpluses should not be allowed to undermine the world price structure.

(b)	In conformity with these aims IFAP should exert the utmost influence with the appropriate international authorities, and through its members, with national governments, in order that such machinery should be in a position to operate before such a situation arises.
(c)	For this purpose the executive committee and the secretary-general are requested to initiate immediate studies in an effort to develop a practical plan capable of accomplishing these aims as nearly as possible.
I am in full accord with those resolutions.^ I feel that unless we can plan, both in Canada and in the international picture, for such agreements as are indicated in those resolutions, we cannot hope for world peace.
I remember that when I was attending high school, one of the things that history taught us *was that the first great war was caused by a fight for world markets. That is what we shall have again unless we can truly say that we are a Christian nation. Unless we can say that we want to move our surplus food from Canada to other countries so that hungry people may get it at reasonable prices, and at the same time protect our producers by handling this matter on a national basis, we cannot truly say we are a Christian nation. If -we once more allow the Winnipeg grain exchange to operate, then once again the producers of this country will be at their mercy.
I want to give full support to this measure. I am convinced that there are many dangers connected with it, simply because we have not seen fit to set up our own internal economy, and to establish appropriate import-export boards to handle such commodities as wheat and others which enter into the field of world trade.

maintopic: APPROVAL OF INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT OPENED FOR SIGNATURE AT WASHINGTON, MARCH 6, 1948
speechtext:
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that we in this group believe in the principle of long-term international wheat agreements. We believe that such agreements are essential to the welfare of both the consuming and the producing nations. We believe they are in the interests of the consuming nations in order to guarantee adequate supplies of food at fair prices, and we believe they are in the interests of the producing nations in order to guarantee markets at fair prices. Moreover, we believe that under such a program it should be possible to build up adequate reserves of food in good crop years to cover shortages that may occur in short crop years. It should be possible, moreover, to build up those reserves without allowing them to be used as an excuse to force prices down, as has invariably been the case under the open market system in the past.

International Wheat Agreement
When the minister spoke in this house upon the introduction of this measure, as reported at page 2004 of Hansard, he concluded with these remarks:
By balancing the interests of both producing countries and consuming countries in an agreement covering the bulk of the world's trade in wheat, the agreement represents a major development in international economic co-operation.
I do not think there is any doubt that this agreement represents a major development in international economic co-operation. It represents many years of striving on the part of farmers to obtain an international agreement. No matter what may be said about this agreement, I think most farmers will be glad to know that for the next five years at least they have a guarantee of a minimum price, even though that price may be considered too low.
On the other hand I think it would be a great mistake for the farmers to place too much reliance upon this agreement, because it has a number of major weaknesses. I wish to deal with what I consider to be two of its chief weaknesses.
In the first place, there is no guarantee that the importing nations will be able to buy the wheat that they undertake to buy under t'he agreement. In the second place, there is no guarantee whatsoever that the interests of the producing and consuming countries under this agreement will be balanced, as stated by the minister.
The main essential of sound international trade policy is the right of a nation to pay for its imports with its exports. No agreement can succeed which flouts that fundamental economic principle. That is why the Bretton Woods agreement has failed, and that is why it will fail in the future, as all previous multilateral trade agreements have failed- because they compel the importing nation to pay either in gold or in the currency of the exporting nation, instead of allowing the importing nation to pay with its own goods.
If the nations desiring our wheat under the agreement are unable to secure dollars, they will be unable to pay for that wheat; and they may very well seek to get that wheat elsewhere, using the currency of soft currency countries. On the other hand they may seek, as they did after the first war, to become more self-sufficient.
It is true that under the agreement provision is made whereby the quota of a country which cannot meet its commitments may be allocated to other countries. But suppose Great Britain were unable to meet its commitments, and we had to redistribute its quota of 170 million bushels; obviously the
whole agreement would collapse. Yet Great Britain has had great difficulty in finding the dollars to pay for food under agreements we have already made with her, and it is probable that that same situation may develop in the future and become aggravated.
Then, on the second point-does the agreement balance the interests of the consuming and producing nations?-I would say that if it does, it will be purely accidental, because the whole international agreement as laid down at the present time is nothing more or less than a gamble. The nations under this agreement are guessing future values instead of establishing them on a basis of fact. By their haphazard methods they may very well discredit what is in reality a sound principle. Because if this agreement fails and becomes discredited, we all realize it will be very difficult to get another wheat agreement in the future.
The agreement establishes the following basis for the price of wheat; For 1948-49 a minimum price of $1.50 and a maximum of $2; that maximum continues throughout the agreement until 1952-53; the minimum price is reduced ten cents each year, so that by 1952-53 the minimum will be only $1.10 a bushel. How do we know that that will be a fair basis or a fair price upon which to establish prices? If the price levels of other goods remain up in 1949, 1950 and 1951, why should the minimum price be dropped ten cents in each of those years? The price level may go higher, or it may drop; but to say that the minimum price shall be dropped ten cents each year, without any regard for general price levels, is gambling upon the future, and it is not a sound basis upon which to establish a minimum price.
On the other hand, if the price level rises, why should the ceiling be held at $2 during that period? Many people today are comparing this agreement with the British wheat agreement. I should like to emphasize one essential difference between this and the British wheat agreement. This wheat agreement is supposed to be a straight business deal between nations, while the British wheat agreement was not. The government asked the house to support the British wheat agreement more or less as a moral obligation, in order that we might give Great Britain wheat at a fair price, or at a low price, having in mind the great sacrifices that country made during the war. At the time the British wheat agreement was discussed in the house, we in this group said that we would support it as a moral obligation, but as a moral obligation of the Canadian people as a whole,

International Wheat Agreement
and that any losses suffered under that agreement should be borne not by the farmers only, but by Canadians as a whole. We pointed out that it would be Canada's responsibility.
On the other hand, at that time the government said that the losses of the first years would be offset by the gains in later years. I do not think anyone would care to argue that way today. It is evident now that as a result of the British wheat agreement the farmers of this country will have suffered losses amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars. I have in my hand a letter I received from H. G. L. Strange, date March 15, 1948, in which he says:
My department has recently figured them out-
He is referring to losses.
-from August 1, 1946 to March 4, 1948. The difference between the $1.55 for our wheat sold to Britain and the price at which our class II wheat was sold 'by the board to all countries of the world comes to $306,62)1,592', and the additional losses for the same period on wheat sold to our millers to be made into bread and flour for domestic consumption comes to $157,338,060 or a total of $463,959,592, because of the low' price set under the British-Canadian wheat agreement. The loss will be still greater I fear by July 31, next, which will be the end of the second year of the British-Canadian wheat agreement.

speechtext:
Yes; therefore we sold her cheap wheat as a moral obligation, and I say it is the responsibility of the Canadian people.

The cost should be borne by the Canadian people, and not by the Canadian farmer, as has been the situation up to the present.
It is evident that if the losses suffered by the farmers during the first two years of the agreement were to be offset, the price of wheat during the last two years would have to fall far below a dollar. That is obviously impossible, in view of the fact that the nations are agreeing to a minimum of $1.50 for this year.
Some may say: You must admit that it was as a result of the British wheat agreement that nations agreed to the new w'heat agreement. But the reason we are getting this new agreement has nothing to do with the British wheat agreement, because Britain was the only country which got cheap wheat, while all other nations had to pay world prices. So that we could have got this agreement just as easily, whether we had embarked upon the British wheat agreement or not. It cannot be argued therefore that this has to be taken in conjunction with the British wheat agreement.
As the Canadian government entered into the British agreement undoubtedly in order to give Great Britain cheap wheat, it is up to the government to pay to the farmers the difference between the price obtained from Great Britain and that obtained for class II wheat. Of course the same applies to wheat sold for domestic consumption, because it is being sold at the same price as wheat sold to Great Britain.
In signing the British wheat agreement and giving Great Britain cheap wheat, the government no doubt expected that the price of wheat would fall. They had in mind what happened after the first great war, and no doubt they expected that the same thing would happen after this war. It is now up to the government to pay the farmers the money they lost in the gamble. I urge the government to stop gambling in that way. Mind you, I am not criticizing the idea of a long-term international wheat agreement, but I am criticizing the basis upon which the price is being established. We feel that in a long-term international agreement the price should be established on the basis of parity rather than by guessing at future values. Under the agreement there is no relationship between the guaranteed price and the future price levels of other commodities.
We feel that an international wheat agreement should be a sound business proposition based upon realities and not upon guesswork. We feel that there is a sound basis for agreement. Nations can agree upon fair prices for the first year; seldom is there any difficulty in arriving at a fair price for the first year.

International Wheat Agreement
because you know the prices of other commodities and you can reach an agreement. But just as soon as you try to set a price for future years you run into guesswork unless you use some yardstick. We insist that in establishing a price for future years it should be tied to the general price level of the importing country; it should be based on the rise and fall of the price level of the importing country. That would unquestionably be parity. Then our exports of wheat to that country would buy from year to year a comparable amount of that country's goods. For instance, if we export wheat to France and in the first year the agreement price is set at 12 per bushel, then the price for future years should be based upon the price level. If the price level in France went up ten per cent, automatically the price of our wheat would go up ten per cent. If the price level in France went down ten per cent, then the price of wheat would go down ten per cent. The result would be that the exports of wheat to that country would bring back the same amount of imports. In other words, you would be establishing the future price upon parity instead of guesswork.
We feel that such a policy would help to insulate the Canadian economy against external fluctuations in the price level, and would thereby facilitate the setting of a parity price for wheat internally, which of course might vary from that obtained under the international wheat agreement. The internal price would not necessarily be the same as the price externally, but there would be a relationship between the price level in Canada and the external price level.
If the objection is raised that that proposal would mean bilateral agreements when we are trying to get multilateral agreements, let me point out that there would be nothing to prevent the exporting countries from trading the credits obtained in any one country for those of another country-that is, where it was not feasible to take payment of goods from the country to which the wheat had been exported. There is nothing unique about the proposal I have been elaborating. It is similar in principle to that which has been proposed for many years by the London, England, chamber of commerce, a body which perhaps has had more experience in international trade than any other commercial body in the world.
There are many points in this agreement which I think need clarification. I understand that the agreement will not be passed this year in the United States, and I cannot see the need for rushing the matter. So far as Great Britain is concerned, we are tied up for another two years, and we would have no difficulty in that regal'd. Therefore I urge the minister to send
this resolution to the banking and commerce committee in order that we may have a thorough discussion of some of the points to which I have referred, and also other points which I have not mentioned.
The question of price is most important. We in this group do not consider that the basis upon which the price in this agreement has been established is sound. It is purely a gamble. It may work out all right, but on the other hand it may place great hardship upon the farmers of this country. No doubt the government hoped that the prices guaranteed in the British wheat agreement would work out fairly well. I have had talks with different members of the government, and they admit frankly that they expected that the world price of wheat would fall. It did not fall, and as a result the British wheat agreement has cost the farmers of this country around half a billion dollars. That is too great a sum to expect any body of workers in this country to pay. The farmers still hope that the government will make up that loss, but so far we have not had any statement.
We should not make a similar mistake with this new agreement. I have indicated one way in which we can avoid doing that-by tying the price of our wheat to the price level of the country to which we export, so that our exports will at all times bring back to this country a comparable amount of imports, which in reality means nothing more or less than parity prices on an international level.
Mr. GORDON B. ISNOR (Halifax): Mr. Speaker, no doubt hon. members from the western prairies will wonder why a member from the maritimes is taking part in a discussion on the wheat agreement, but I can assure them that this wheat agreement is of real interest to all parts of Canada, particularly the eastern section, of which I have the honour to represent one portion.
The international wheat agreement is really a sales agreement which has been entered into by thirty-six countries, thirty-three of which are importers and three of which are exporters. I was at a loss to understand the remark of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) to the effect that there were too few exporting countries in the agreement. I would have thought that the fact that there were just three exporting countries would make our position that much stronger, because we would have thirty-three countries to which to sell. In making a sales agreement of any kind the endeavour is usually to cover as great a field and to secure as many customers as possible.
I rose more particularly to discuss the matter of transportation. On June 11, when the estimates of the bureau of statistics were

International Wheat Agreement
under consideration, I endeavoured to bring up this matter of transportation as it affects the wheat agreement. I was quite properly called to order by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), and I accepted the ruling that I was wrong in attempting to bring it up at that time. I am therefore taking advantage -of this opportunity to place before the minister and the house one or two points that I have in mind.
The first point I should like to draw to the attention of the minister has to do with the basis upon which the prices are established, that is, No. 1 northern in store Fort William-Port Arthur. While the prices are based on Fort William-Port Arthur, I think there should be a definite relationship to the Atlantic and Pacific ports for shipping purposes. We should at all times have a sufficient quantity on hand at those ports to avoid a situation similar to that which arose last year and which was referred to in the British house by Conservative members of parliament.
I shall refer to that in just a moment, but before doing so I should like to ask the minister to take into consideration one or two points which I wish to mention specifically in connection with the clauses of the agreement.
The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), who is always interesting and presents an intelligent picture of matters pertaining to wheat and the west generally, is in accord, I was pleased to note, with the general principles of this agreement, and favours the action being taken by the government. From a business standpoint Canada is indeed fortunate in being able to enter into an agreement under which she will sell twenty-three fiftieths of the total 500 million bushels.
I wish to refer the minister to clause 7 of the agreement, to be found on page 10, which deals with the records to be kept. It says.
The council shall prescribe the records which shall be kept of the transactions reported in accordance with the provisions of paragraph 6 of this article.
I am anxious to know whether that clause will be interpreted as applying to the total grain on hand in the various elevators, including, as we would naturally expect, the elevators at Atlantic ports. To us that is an important thing which should not be overlooked in this agreement. It should be clearly understood that the records shall be interpreted as referring to the elevators at the shipping ports, particularly in the extreme eastern section of our country.
I want to couple with that the definition of "f.o.b." in article XIX on page 34 of the agreement. Paragraph 7 of the definitions says:
" 'F.o.b.' means free on board." If that means

the price quoted at any Atlantic or Pacific port, it answers one of the questions I have in my mind, and perhaps the minister would be good enough to say later whether or not my interpretation is correct.
Paragraph 11 of the definitions defines "marketing costs" thus:
"Marketing costs" means all usual charges incurred in procurement, marketing, chartering, and forwarding.
I again contend that this wheat should be transported direct to the nearest port to Europe, in other words to the nearest port on the Atlantic which will give the cheapest transportation by water. I need not point out to the minister that Halifax to Liverpool is the shortest route; under this agreement, therefore, the port of Halifax will expect a greater shipment of wheat than we have had in the past.
Paragraph 13 of the definitions defines "stocks":
"Stocks" means in Australia, Canada, and the United States of America the total of the stocks of old wheat held at the end of their respective crop-years in all elevators, warehouses, and mills.
And so forth. Again I urge upon the minister that he make use of that clause to see that we on the Atlantic coast have our elevators at all times filled to take care of the requirements of ships which enter our ports from time to time and which sometimes have been unable to procure the shipments we so urgently require.
This shortage of wheat shipments from Atlantic ports was brought up in the British house, as reported in the Halifax Herald of June 8, 1948:
Critical of at least two phases of the British government's policy of buying wheat in bulk to meet national needs, the Conservative party in Britain raises one point of particular interest to Nova Scotia generally and to the port of Halifax in particular.
After discussing the arrangements covering a four-year period, in the course of which a tribute is paid to the Canadian farmer who receives less than the market price for his wheat, the party's statement says Canada fell short on deliveries in 1945, though other countries received proportionately more than their share. Then it adds:
"When the St. Lawrence froze, the government had to make frantic efforts to ship wheat from Pacific ports, which must have meant an addition of 10 to 15 cents a bushel to the cost."
I think the minister was aware of that situation last year. It was treated with a certain amount of humour by members from the east, but at the same time it was serious. Of course there is no such thing as the freezing of Halifax harbour. The same thing applies to some extent to Saint John, but so far as Halifax is

International Wheat Agreement
concerned we do not know what it is to have an ice-bound harbour. I urge upon the minister that he take into consideration and make provision in the agreement by which we shall have proper protection.
The article goes on to refer to that official statement, that we were unable to ship from eastern Atlantic ports, and says:
At that the gap was such that wheat purchases had to be made in the Argentine at $3 a bushel!
Nova Scotia will recall the situation, as it developed in the autumn of 1946, as it was disclosed in the British House of Commons by Food Minister Strachey. He said at that time that he had pressed the Canadian government to hasten deliveries. He said that he had urged the Canadian government to use Canadian Atlantic ports because shipping was short and it was costly in terms of shipping alone to move the wheat by way of the Pacific and Panama.
I recall that at that time I took the liberty of personally wiring the Hon. Anthony Eden, pointing out that Halifax harbour was always free of ice, that I hoped this fact would be made clear to the British food minister and others interested, and that we would have no more official statements such as that so far as Halifax was concerned. The article goes on:
But no wheat moved. Finally the situation became so grim that the British government had to appeal to the United States transportation authorities to expedite shipments of Canadian wheat by way of United States railways and ports.
Again I take exception. There is no need of that. From time to time I have advocated, and I emphasize this point, that there should be a clause in every wheat sale agreement made by Canada that the shipments be made through our own Canadian ports. If we are selling the goods, surely we are in a position to say: Yes, we will give you the agreed price at an Atlantic port. I would urge upon the minister that he take that into his serious consideration as an amendment to the present agreement.
Again I say I am pleased that Canada is not waiting for the United States but is now taking steps to seek the approval which I feel sure the house will give to this agreement. Some have advocated that we should wait until the United States has made its position clear. But I say this is a good, clear-cut sales agreement, covering a four-year period, and representing 230 million bushels of wheat, and that we should by all means take advantage of the agreement by approving it as soon as possible.
Hon. members have brought to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) this matter of shipment through
Canadian ports. Had the present Minister of Trade and Commerce held the office that he holds today we might have had more definite action, and action which would have helped us. No explanation was ever forthcoming from Ottawa in respect of the complaint I raise as to why shipments of wheat were made over United States railways and through United States ports. Perhaps even at this late date the Minister of Trade and Commerce will tell us why that happened, and guard against such occurrences in the future.
I think I have accomplished what I had in mind. I did not deal with the question of the price of wheat. I am not in a position to do that. There are wheat growers in the house who know whether these prices are fair and whether a long-term policy is a good one. I ask the minister to give every consideration to the transportation of Canadian wheat through Canadian ports.

maintopic: APPROVAL OF INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT OPENED FOR SIGNATURE AT WASHINGTON, MARCH 6, 1948
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with some interest to the presentation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) this morning in respect to the international wheat agreement. He pointed out that it was necessary for the various countries to ratify the agreement not later than July 1 in order that it may operate for the 1948 crop year. He said that this agreement provided for a ceiling price of $2 a bushel, and that the floor price ranged from $1.50 down to $1.10 a bushel. That is not the net figure to the farm producer. I would judge it would average about 20 cents a bushel less than that, net to the farmer, if the agreement is carried out.
It seems rather strange that we should be tying into an agreement such as this at a time when there is a great scarcity of wheat in the country and prevailing wheat prices are much higher than $2 a bushel on the world market. In fact during the past year wheat has sold at considerably over $3.40 a bushel, which is a great deal higher than $2 a bushel.
In recent days I have been in touch with a number of millers, especially in western Canada, whose plants are closed down because they cannot purchase wheat to mill into flour. This is a serious state of affairs for these mill operators. The majority of the small private millers have their plants actually closed today because they cannot purchase wheat in the country with which to make flour. That is also true of the flour export business. It proves that at this particular time there is a great demand and a great shortage of wheat in this country.
The minister said that Australia and Canada would handle all their wheat through their wheat board. That means that under present

International Wheat Agreement
government legislation, all wheat in Canada will be handled compulsorily through the Canadian wheat board. The farmer has no choice other than to deliver his wheat to the wheat board at the prices set by the board. Of course these prices are agreed to or set by the cabinet committee, which is in charge of the Canadian wheat board. I repeat, it is a compulsory method; the farmer has no choice. On the other hand, the United States government has told its people that the open market will be continued in that country, and if the price in that county, or the world price, is considerably over $2 a bushel, the wheat producer of the United States of America will receive the existing price at whatever figure prevails over the $2. In fact, in that respect the United States Department of Agriculture on May 25 announced a government loan or support price for the 1948 crop as follows: Chicago, S2.25 a bushel; Minneapolis, $2.22 a bushel; Kansas City, $2.20 a bushel, and Portland, Oregon, S2.15 a bushel. This means an average loan rate on wheat to farmers on their farms of $1.96. The farmer in the United States is guaranteed that, no matter where the price may fall, because he receives the loan, and he receives on top of that at a later date whatever is obtained over and above that figure. He may receive a great deal more than the $1.96 that he is guaranteed. Therefore hon. gentlemen will readily see how much more fortunate the wheat producer in the United States is than the farmer in this country is and has been throughout the crop years.
I have to agree almost entirely with the speech delivered by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Queleh) this morning. He handled the situation very well. I agreed with him when he said that the wheat farmers of this country have made altogether too great a contribution to the consumers of Great Britain, and also to the consumers of Canada. He pointed out that it was not a straight business deal, that we had to do something to assist Britain. With that we all agree, and I have always agreed that that contribution should be made. Let me repeat what I have often said: the contribution should have been borne by all the taxpayers of this country, and not by one class of people.
In another debate on May 26 I gave a list of figures showing what it would cost the farm producers of this country. For the first nine months of 1947-48 crop year alone, under the United Kingdom wheat agreement, our farmers lost $191,891,763. That is the difference between what they received and what they might have received, had they received the average class II price of wheat. The prices were averaged month by month from August 1, 1947, to

April of this year-nine months. On the same basis, on the flour and wheat used for consumption in Canada they lost another $8,401,104, a total of $274,292,867 in the first nine months of this crop year. No other producers in Canada are asked to contribute on that basis, nor were they throughout the war years. That policy is continuing, and we do not know how long it may continue in the future. It has been most unfair.
I also pointed out, then, that if the proposed wheat agreement went into effect, it would be absolute proof that the farmers, who continue in the future to operate under this policy would never have an opportunity to regain that very great loss running into many hundreds of millions of dollars. I am satisfied that that is the situation. I agree that over the past fifteen years these nations have been trying to work out an international wheat agreement, and that many farmers of this country want something of that kind. I do not think any farmer will be satisfied wdth these prices under these conditions.
I remember the argument we had on the United Kingdom wheat agreement. Along with many other hon. members of this party I argued that with the rising costs at that time it would be disastrous for the farm producers of this country, and as I read the statements over and over again I find that every word of the prophecy has come true, and much more. The costs of the wheat producers are rising daily. Not long ago an average increase of 21 per cent across the board was granted in freight rates. I will admit that that increase does not apply to wheat, but this parliament permitted that increase.

Parliament stood by the board which passed it. Parliament did not do anything about it. The board, under this government, passed the freight rate increase. I agree that all of the opposition parties tried their best to prevent it and have something done about it. I am sure we have not yet reached the peak. Every few months sees an increase in the cost of farm machinery.
I want to see the farm worker get everything possible. I have always been in favour of the

International Wheat Agreement
workers of the country obtaining all they can, but all these things enter into the cost of production. According to the bureau of statistics, the farm labourer receives three times as much in farm wages today as he received in 1939. There are many other items I might mention, the prices of which the economists of this country say have not yet reached the peak in Canada. These must all be taken into consideration.
I say, therefore, that when you ask people who have borne such a heavy loss since 1939, and who are bearing the burden today, to sign this international wheat agreement, under which the maximum they will receive will be $2-and even that not net, since it will be twenty cents less than that, with a minimum of $1.10-you are providing that these wheat producers shall continue to suffer this great loss for many years to come.
I am sure that, while they want an international wheat agreement, the people who ask for one will not be as satisfied with the prices set forth in that article. If the government are determined to ratify this agreement at the present time, I must say that I see no urgency about it; because, as was pointed out by my leader this morning, the United States, through its senate committee, is now considering the matter, and if that committee reports favourably, -which I doubt,.it will require a vote of two-thirds of the senate of the United States before the agreement can become law. Only ten days are left to the first of July, and according to press reports they do not intend to have a report in before that date. Therefore I fail to see the urgency of ratifying this agreement.
Australia has ratified the agreement with the proviso that its signature stands only if the United States government ratifies it by the first of July. Surely, if this government is determined to ratify the agreement at this time, it will adopt a similar proviso. I suggest to the minister that he amend the resolution by adding a clause, "subject to ratification and approval by the senate or other competent legislative body of the United States of America". I hope the minister will do that. I was prepared to move such an amendment, but I have suggested similar amendments in the past and they have been ruled out of order at a stage in debate corresponding to this. I understand that this resolution is not going through committee stage. We are merely discussing it on this motion. Judging from past rulings of the Chair, I think I would be out of order in moving such an amendment, but I appeal to the minister as earnestly as I can to insert in the resolution a proviso such as I have suggested. I do not think the agreement should be ratified without some such safeguard. I hope the minister will adopt that suggestion.
I have no wish to take up much more time.
I have pointed out how unfair it will be to the farm producers of the country.

maintopic: APPROVAL OF INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT OPENED FOR SIGNATURE AT WASHINGTON, MARCH 6, 1948
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the agreement before us is to assure supplies of wheat to thirty-three countries and to assure a market to the three countries which, under the agreement at the present time, will be the producer countries. I would like to point out to the last speaker, who suggested that Canadian legislation will be passed, subject to ratification of the agreement by the United States government, that at page 36 of the international wheat agreement there is this provision:
This agreement shall be subject to formal acceptance by the signatory governments. Instruments of acceptance shall be deposited with the government of the United States of America by July 1, 1948'; provided, however, that an additional period shall be allorved by the council for the deposit of instruments of acceptance on behalf of those importing countries which are prevented by a recess of their respective legislatures from accepting this agreement by July 1, 1948,

International Wheat Agreement
We support any move which will assist in the proper distribution of foodstuffs throughout the world. It is significant that the international federation of agricultural producers of the world has supported this agreement. It is an effort on the part of producers and consumers to distribute properly the essentials of life without the gambling that goes with the open market system, of which we have had too much in the past, and still have. We regret the news items which indicate that this agreement will not likely go into effect at all because the congress of the United States will not sign it.
The world is moving away from the old ideas which prevailed in connection with the grain exchange open market and the cotton exchange. It is moving towards the place where distribution of the essentials of adequate living shall be made to all people, and privileged groups shall not have the power to gamble with these essentials and extract for their own benefit large profits to the detriment of producer and consumer. Because, therefore, this is a step in that direction, we support it with everything we have.
World prices are becoming a myth. People talk about the losses Canada has suffered because of failure to sell commodities at world prices. These have not been world prices. What are world prices? Prices quoted on the Chicago stock exchange are not world prices; and as for what Canada has lost in this regard, I would like those people who have been talking about the loss to Canadians in the past under the United Kingdom agreement to compare the prices at which producers in Canada sold their commodities on the grain exchange with prices on the world market over the past fifty years, adding up all that was produced and sold at the low prices to the line elevators. Compare the prices there with the prices at which the Winnipeg grain exchange sold the produce, not to mention prices which might have prevailed in the United States. The Canadian producer never got the grain exchange prices of the United States.
This agreement commits Canada to a five-year distribution or export of 230 million bushels a year, the United States to 185 million bushels a year, and Australia to 85 million bushels a year. The producers support this principle, because, in spite of the fact that prices are low, there is an element of stability which they never had before.
I am not satisfied with the prices, cost of production being what it is today. The Canadian producer stands to lose heavily by it if costs continue to rise. I would point out,

however, that there is an arrangement for adjustment in the last three years of the agreement. The world has not been producing foodstuffs to the extent that we expected after the last war, but it is possible that within the next five years we shall see a great deal of production. I do not think the farmers should have to take the risk of the loss involved in the difference between their cost of production and the prices which may prevail here. I believe, with the hon. member for Acadia, that Canadian prices should be tied up with cost of production and commodity prices within our own country. That is a valuable suggestion, and I agree that it would be a good thing for the Canadian government to guarantee the Canadian producer a tying-up of the domestic market prices and the foreign market prices so as to afford him cost of production with a little margin. If we have not this agreement, are we going to allow the grain exchange to handle our produce? That is the alternative to which the average producer objects, and that is why he supports this move in the direction of stability such as he has not had in the past.
Those who oppose the agreement do not offer any satisfactory alternative. If things are left as they are, what guarantee has the farmer? He will go back to the old conditions. The grain exchange give him a price one day and get him to deliver his produce. He has now sold it. They manipulate the market, and the price goes up. The grain exchange buyer sells the commodity to the consumer at a high price, pockets the difference, so the Canadian consumer and producer lose. That is what makes producers in Canada and producers all over the world support something which will give them stability. On the basis of that principle we are supporting this measure with everything we 'have. If those who oppose it have something else, let them bring their proposition forward and let us support it.

maintopic: APPROVAL OF INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT OPENED FOR SIGNATURE AT WASHINGTON, MARCH 6, 1948
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock I was just going to deal with one or two matters referred to by the minister. Press reports this morning indicate that both houses of the United States congress have risen, with the result that it would appear completely improbable, if not impossible, that the agree-
International Wheat Agreement

ment will be ratified by the United States; therefore there will be no sufficient degree of ratification by the signatory powers before the deadline of July 1.
The United States senate will probably have a committee dealing with this matter; nevertheless it cannot be dealt with by the whole senate. I notice the minister said that the senate of the United States had the matter in hand. This only serves to strengthen the argument we have made today, that there is no haste in dealing with the matter, particularly in the dying days of the session.
I agree, and I think hon. members of this party agree, with what was well said by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), when he pointed out that the proper way to dispose of this resolution would be not to pass it now but to have it referred to the committee on banking and commerce, there to be further studied and dealt with. That is what we now urge upon the government.
I should like to deal with another statement of the minister. He said that the price range really operates to give importers the right to buy, and exporters are obliged to sell at ceiling prices, if a deal can be consummated at those figures. On the other hand, importers are obliged to buy, and exporters have the right to sell at the floor price. In other words I do not see where there is any certainty about it. There is still the matter of dealing between exporting and importing countries as to the price to be charged between the maximum and minimum prices each year. I maintain that the price spread between maximum and minimum is completely out of line with the necessities of the occasion. I do not think this should be. Actual sales, if there are any, and if this agreement ever comes into force-which I doubt-will likely take place somewhere between the maximum and the minimum in each year. And as between exporting and importing countries, if we cannot agree on a price between maximum and minimum, there will be no deal, unless the importers will say to the exporters: We will give you the maximum; or the exporter will say to the importers: We will accept the minimum.
In other words, if there is any certainty about this entire agreement, it is that it is completely uncertain. There is no stability and no certainty. And there is another uncertainty in it too. With that large spread between maximum and minimum, large exporting countries outside the agreement altogether can put the pressure on the market and without any question can put our countries in such a position that if they wish to deal at all

with importing countries, they will have to deal with those importing countries at the very minimum rates set out in the agreement. If we are driven to the expedient of relying on these minimum rates, there is no minimum in the agreement which by any stretch of the imagination can be deemed proper and sufficient for our farmers and for our people generally in western Canada. There is the great danger, I repeat, that countries which are normally exporters of wheat can put such pressure on the importing countries, by means of offerings, as to compel us, if we wish to deal at all, to accept the minimum. In other words, instead of helping ourselves we shall establish a minimum and betray ourselves.
The minister did not tell us this morning- at least I did not hear him tell us-the number of countries which have initialled the agreement. I believe it was twenty-two or twenty-eight.
