maintopic: APPROVAL OF INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT OPENED FOR SIGNATURE AT WASHINGTON, MARCH 6, 1948
speechtext:
Perhaps the minister will tell- us, when he closes the debate, how many of the importing countries have already ratified the agreement. In any event, the minister and I are united in this, that if the United States does not ratify it, the agreement will not be of any worthwhile benefit and will not come into operation.
When the minister speaks again he should clear up for us unequivocally -this question: If we sign this agreement, and if it is filed with the registering party, the United States government, are we bound by its terms to offer our wheat for export regardless of how many importing and exporting countries actually ratify the agreement by legislation? There are so many pitfalls which have not yet been explained that it is the part of folly, in my humble judgment at least, for us blindly to ratify this agreement, simply to be the first, second or third among the countries ratifying it. It affects a commodity that is important to our whole economy, and we should give it the closest study.
Tire trouble is, particularly with those of us who come from the west, that we still remember the scare we got in 1929 and succeeding years when huge surpluses were piled up and had to be offered at almost fire-sale prices. The government and its advisers, perhaps, and many of us in the west, are fearful that again we may have a surplus piled up at low prices.

International Wheat Agreement
I submit that this agreement, and some other agreements which have been made with regard to wheat, have been entered into because of that great and underlying fear. We should not enter into improvident agreements with respect to wheat, because while an ageement may be right in principle, it may be very wrong in details as to prices and the like.
The time has come when, as a large exporting country, we should take our courage in our hands in dealing with our wheat supplies and endeavour to get a decent price for our farmers. So far as the United States farmer is concerned, probably this does give him some security. I understand their government will continue to buy wheat on the open market, and anyway their exportable surplus is not a substantial part of their crop. But even then they will be getting more benefit than our farmers will be getting, unless our government also provides that if our farmers have to sell their wheat cheaper, they will protect the farmers by .buying it in the open market, or at least giving an additional price to the farmers for their grain; because our farmers cannot get along at present proposed prices.
Even if that were done, there are two things to consider. The first is that our farmers took the low prices at a time when- they could have had high prices, and when the United States farmers got their high prices. It is not so bad for the United States farmers to say: Oh, well; we had good prices during the war which the Canadian farmers did not have, and we will now take low prices for security's sake. Our farmers had to take low prices, and now we do not get any more security or any greater price-in fact not as much as the United States farmers will get if their government enters into this agreement.
It is true that most of our people want some sort of agreement like this. It is the duty of the house to see that we do not ignore the body of the agreement that we sign, just to secure an agreement which we approve in principle; let us also seek an agreement that will be fair to the people who are chiefly affected.
I would like the minister to say, when he speaks in closing the debate, what the effect will be if no countries ratify it other than those who have already done so. Is it or is it not to be enforced this year? According to the agreement, it should be enforced this year, but it cannot be enforced until it is ratified. In order that there may be no confusion I think the minister should tell us whether this agreement will be in operation this year if we ratify it. How many nations must ratify it before it will be in force?
The various countries can get out from under if they have exchange difficulties. For
instance, if Great Britain decides that she is having exchange difficulties, and goes to the council and says that she has a contract under the agreement to buy 180 million bushels of wheat, the council can reallocate that wheat. But I ask the minister to whom could they reallocate Britain's huge share of 180 million of the 500 million bushels under the new agreement? Who would have the money to buy Britain's ISO million bushels if Britain cannot? What countries among the thirty-three can be expected not to have exchange difficulties? These important problems should be settled, and that is why this resolution should be referred to a committee, as I have suggested.
There are no means of enforcing the agreement. It depends simply on the honour or good faith of the countries involved.
There is another point which has not so far been referred to. Article VI, section 9, restricts to some extent our own control over the domestic price of our grain, and perhaps over grain which we might sell outside the ambit of this agreement.
The agreement presumes that there will be disputes, because elaborate machinery is to be set up for the settlement of disputes between countries. I contend that the elaborate and roundabout and indefinite machinery that is to be set up will not settle any disputes. If there is a dispute, it will involve delay in the marketing of our grain, and before these tortuous methods of arriving at a settlement are carried through to a logical conclusion, our grain will be piling up. In the meantime our farmers will have no money, and there will be the gravest insecurity.
Under an annex to one of the articles in the agreement we undertake to retain at the end of each crop year 70,000,000 bushels of old wheat in reserve. Will that 70,000,000 bushels include what we have to keep in reserve for domestic requirements, or will it be in addition to those requirements? If so, it will be most difficult for us to carry out that section of the agreement. I should like that question cleared up when the minister replies.
Article XVI deals with expenses of the secretariat, council and so on, which are to be apportioned among the different governments according to the percentage in which they share in the exports, and so on. Those expenses will be paid first by the government, but will they then be charged up against the operations of the wheat board? I hope they will not constitute an additional burden upon the western Canadian farmers.
Article XX provides that the United States or any other nation may ask for additional

International Wheat Agreement
time if their legislature is in recess. How long must we wait until the various recesses have expired? How long will it be before our farmers know whether we are to have this agreement? How many legislatures are now in recess, and when do those recesses conclude? When will this agreement come into force? When will the western Canadian farmers know that their grain is to move to the markets of the world under this agreement?
Even the importing countries seem to be getting a little shaky about whether this agreement will come into force. Why are we spending time debating an agreement that might never see the light of day? Are we doing it simply for the sake of notoriety and publicity?
If this agreement comes into force, the undertakings of the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), both on the hustings and in this house, will go by the board. Under the United Kingdom agreement, undoubtedly the grain produced by the fanners of western Canada has been sold at a lower price, but the minister has promised that the farmers would be reimbursed in the final years of the United Kingdom contract by being given a price exceeding the world price. If this agreement is to be put into force, I ask the minister to tell us how the farmers are to be reimbursed for the low prices they accepted for their grain during the war years. At the best they can be reimbursed only to the extent of $70,000,000 to $100,000,000, or possibly $140,000,000, even if grain goes down to the minimum provided by this agreement. They cannot possibly get those hundreds of millions of dollars which they have lost already and which they were told would be accounted for in the last great accounting under the United Kingdom agreement. It looks to me as though that great accounting which we were promised has already been submerged in the Atlantic ocean under the terms of this new wheat agreement.
If this agreement comes into force, there will never be enough as between the United Kingdom and our government to reimburse the western farmers for the losses they took during the war when they compulsorily delivered their wheat at less than its true value. The problem will be solved for the government if this trade agreement is finally adopted.
I agree with some of the other speakers, and I think it is a self-evident truth, that the prices of our grain have been fixed at the lowest point that was discussed by the

importing and exporting countries. I am not minimizing the difficulty faced by the government in marketing our grain. The thirty-three importing countries would try to get grain as cheaply as they could, while the government would try to bargain to get rid of as much grain as they could. But- apparently this government, along with its agricultural advisers, are still labouring under the delusion from which they suffered in the days when we had those terrible prices and those large grain surpluses.
Frankly, I hesitate to vote against this resolution. I have studied the agreement as well as I can. We can only study it to the best of our individual ability. I submit again that a matter as important as this should be sent to one of the standing committees- I suggest the committee on banking and commerce-so that we can get all the facts and not have to decide a matter so important, not only to the farmers of western Canada, but to their children and their children's children. The government should give us every bit of available information when they ask us to make such an important decision as this.
There is no need to be hasty. If we go on like this, we will regret our haste. I cannot see how any harm could be done to any person, to importers or exporters, or to any government, or how our position could be in any way prejudiced, if this matter were referred to a committee where all the facts could be brought out and we could ascertain whether there was any danger in delay. We from western Canada do not want to do anything that would be prejudicial to the farmers of western Canada. We do not want to be hurried into a decision unless we are confident that it is the right one. Without a full knowledge of the facts, and without further study, I shall be inclined to vote against this resolution unless the minister agrees to refer it to a committee.

maintopic: APPROVAL OF INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT OPENED FOR SIGNATURE AT WASHINGTON, MARCH 6, 1948
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe the people of Canada realize the importance of this international wheat agreement. Many people do not realize how great a loss the farmers of western Canada have suffered through the British wheat agreement, As has been often stated, we have not objected to the low price which was given to Britain under that agreement, because we realized that there was a moral responsibility, which was pointed out at the time. But it should have been the responsibility of the whole Canadian people to supply that wheat to Britain, and I ask whether it is the inten-

International Wheat Agreement
tion of the government to make good to the farmers the loss imposed upon them by that agreement.
It would seem that by this international agreement we are again tying up the farmers of the prairie provinces, because in it no consideration is given to the costs of production to which the farmers of Canada may be subjected-no consideration whatsoever.
Under the terms of the agreement the minimum price for the first year of the contract will be S1.50 per bushel, and in the remaining years the price will be allowed to drop ten cents a bushel. Will the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) tell us on what sound business these stipulations are made, and the reason for the $2 per bushel maximum price in the contract, which runs for five years? That price is much better than the price that prevailed during the depression years, but in view of the market price for class II wheat, even the price of $2 a bushel is not as high as it should be. Why should our farmers be deprived of the rightful price to which they are entitled for their produce?
It has been agreed by everybody that our farmers have been taking the rap since 1929, almost twenty years. Why tie them up again for another five years under this agreement? The farmers are not against a long-term agreement in respect of wheat and perhaps other farm products, but I do not know of any farmer who will sacrifice price just for the sake of a long-term agreement.
The member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) placed our position clearly before the house this morning, and I do not think I can improve on what he said. It was stated this morning that the British wheat agreement in the first two years will cost the prairie farmers half a billion dollars on wheat alone. That is quite a lot of money. Many people do not realize that while there was a price ceiling on coarse grains, it was based on the price of wheat in the British wheat agreement. They do not realize that the price of our pork and beef was based on the price of coarse grains, thus tying the price of all these products to the price of wheat in the British wheat agreement. That has cost the farmer many more millions of dollars than anybody in the house realizes, and here we are being tied again by a contract which is vague in the extreme. To me it does not look like good business.
I ask the minister whether he is agreeable to sending this measure to the banking and commerce committee, where definite information can be secured so that we shall know what we are doing. This agreement is of vital interest to all the people, not to the farmers
of Canada alone. The money the farmers received for their products is spent in Canada, and for that reason all Canada benefits when our agriculture is prosperous.

maintopic: APPROVAL OF INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT OPENED FOR SIGNATURE AT WASHINGTON, MARCH 6, 1948
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realize that this question of an international wheat agreement is essentially a western problem, but as it will affect the economy of the whole of Canada I should like to say a few words about it.
The agreement involves 500 million bushels of wheat a year, of which Canada's share will be 230 million bushels, or 46 per cent; the share of the United States 185 million bushels or 37 per cent, and the share of Australia, 85 million bushles, or 17 per cent. So far the minister has not told us how many governments have ratified this agreement. He has told us that Australia has, with a rider that if it is not ratified by the United States the agreement will be voided by Australia. There are two great wheat-producing countries still outside of the agreement. Probably 800 million bushels of wheat is the yearly world trading figure, but the total production is much greater. What will happen if 100 million bushels, or even 50 million bushels of this 800 million, are traded outside of this agreement at five cents a bushel less than the amount stipulated in the agreement? Does the minister think that the nations approving the agreement Will hold to it and pay the extra price in the face of that offer? How can we expect a foreign government, or even a government of a sister nation in the commonwealth, to guarantee our growers what we feel to be fair prices?
I contend that only our own government in co-operation with our own growers can possibly bring about this stability. 'Obviously in any agreement of this kind which seeks to stabilize World prices, the importing nations must realize that they will have to pay a little more than the world price when there is a large surplus of wheat in the world. Why? Because under the agreement they are buying wheat at 'less than the world price. The ceiling price in the agreement is thirteen per cent below the world price of wheat today. Why is the ceiling not fixed nearer to the world price?
I wonder whether any labour union in this country would sign an agreement for five years with the maximum wage twenty-two per cent below existing rates? I base these figures on the fact that the guarantee to the farmer will net to him only $180 of the existing $2.31 world price, or approximately 22 per cent below the world price. Would a union sign an agreement on the basis of a possible drop of forty-five per cent in wages within the next
International Wheat Agreement

five years? Would any manufacturer sign such an agreement? It is my belief that they would not do so. Why, therefore, should we ask the farmers of this country to do something that we know the unions or the manufacturers would not do?
I believe, and it is the belief of many hon. members who have spoken in his debate, that during the war the farmers of this country took a great deal less than the world price for their products. In view of the fact that the farmers have taken this loss during the past five years, it would appear to me that the government is asking us to ratify, in the dying days of the session, an agreement which asks the farmers to turn the other cheek and let it be slapped also.

speechtext:
Before the question is put I should like to ask the minister, who will close the debate, to explain the basis upon which the agreement was arrived at, in respect to the actual amount that is to be paid to farmers for the wheat. Was any thought given to the price in Canada itself? It is conceivable, for example, that our farmers might not be able to produce wheat at SI.10 a bushel if the costs of their production were as high, or any thing like as high, as they are today. Therefore it would appear to me that we ought to have some assurance that the farmer's costs will go down as it is expected the price of wheat will go down. I would like the minister to give us some idea of how the amounts to be paid were arrived at. In asking that question I wish to say that, like hon. members around me, I am in full accord with the principle involved in this agreement, and should like to support it, because I believe it aims at stability for agriculture.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Charlton) bemoaned the prices that the farmers received during the war. If we were to abandon all this regulation and price fixing, would he guarantee to the farmers that two, three or five years from now they will be getting as much for their wheat as they are now? He would have to take a great risk to do that. This is the only sensible way to go about the thing; but, I do insist that there ought to be some relationship between the costs of producing wheat in Canada and the floor price which is expected under this agreement.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: APPROVAL OF INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT OPENED FOR SIGNATURE AT WASHINGTON, MARCH 6, 1948
speechtext:
As hon. members are probably aware, the question before us is

whether we shall or shall not ratify an agreement that has already been made. The agreement was made by delegates of the government, among whom were included the leaders of the three largest wheat marketing organizations in Canada, as well as other men whose reputation as market experts is well established. The unanimous recommendation of Canada's delegates was that the agreement be ratified, as being in the best interests of the Canadian producer. It is significant that the favourable report was not confined to farm organizations in Canada. The leading farm organizations in the United States also recommended to their government that the agreement be ratified. The leading farm organizations of the United Kingdom made the same recommendation to their government. The farm organizations of other countries supported this agreement as being a satisfactory outcome of the efforts of the thirty-six countries which during the past several years have met together in attempts to bring about stability in international wheat trading.
What is the purpose of the agreement? The purpose is to take out a mutual insurance policy. The three producing countries obtain a firm guarantee, first, that they will be able to dispose of the quantities allocated to them under the agreement-in the case of Canada 230 million bushels-and second that they will be able to dispose of that quantity of wheat at a price. It is interesting to hear people laugh off the idea that there may be surpluses in this country, and that there may be difficulty in disposing of surplus wheat. Memories are very short. I was around in the thirties and I know that the most difficult problem of the country in those days was the disposal of our wheat. I know that if any minimum price had been available there would not have been much question as to what the minimum was; if we could have moved the quantity and got any price that seemed reasonable even in those days, that privilege would have been a very welcome insurance policy indeed.
As I say, the insurance policy for the producing countries is that they will be able tc sell a definite quantity of wheat at a definite price. The insurance to the consuming countries is that they will be able to buy a definite quantity of wheat at a maximum price of $2 a bushel. As I say, the experts of all these countries believed that that is a desirable arrangement. I believe it is a desirable insurance policy. I believe that it will do a great deal to stabilize world markets and world price. I believe that Canada should ratify the agreement.

International Wheat Agreement
The question has been raised as to how many countries have ratified the agreement. I cannot say the number; I do not know how many. The date of ratification is the first day of July, and we have not as yet reached that date. We have had informal but definite advice to the effect that the United Kingdom intends to ratify the agreement. Several countries on the continent already have ratified the agreement. Australia has done so. The United States senate has adjourned temporarily without ratifying the agreement, and it is obvious that that country will not ratify it before July 1, but indications are that there is a fair chance that it will be ratified later this year.
As far as the position of the Canadian farmer is concerned, based on whether the agreement is or is not ratified within the next month, may I say that it does not make the slightest difference. Canada's export of wheat is contracted for, for the 1948 and 1949 crops.
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Miller) says it is obvious that the promises of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and the promises of the Minister of Agriculture of the United Kingdom, would not be carried out if the agreement was signed. I may tell him that he is mistaken about that. Conversations have taken place with the United Kingdom government, and it is clearly understood between the two parties to the United Kingdom wheat agreement that the settlement of the current wheat agreement will be made whether the multilateral agreement is signed or not.
It is all very well for hon. members to make speeches about the price of wheat, and to compare the prices obtained under the Canada-United Kingdom agreement with the domestic price in the Chicago market; for the latter is the price they are talking about. They can call it the price of No. 2 wheat if they like. The price of No. 2 wheat has been the price in the Chicago domestic market. Our No. 2 wheat price is the quotation from day to day on the Chicago grain exchange. The quantity of No. 2 wheat that Canada had to sell was small, and as a price had to be fixed, the day to day Chicago price was adopted as reasonable in the circumstances. We know that dentists, doctors, oil men and persons engaged in various professions were dabbling in the Chicago market at that time, and that the United States government was itself alarmed at speculation in that market. Nevertheless hon. members opposite like to talk about $3.20 wheat and compare that with the price obtained for Canadian wheat. We never hear the fact mentioned that the price already paid the western farmer for the 1945 Canadian crop is higher than that obtained for the 1945 crop 5849-355
by any other country in the world, and the final payment on that crop has not yet been determined.
No one knows what will be the final price
for the pool wheat of the crops of 1945, 1946, 1947, 1948 and 1949, and I suggest it might be well to wait for the determination of that price before comparisons are made. I say that any man who attempts to base a comparison on the peak Chicago price for domestic United States wheat is attempting to deceive his listeners, and I say that without qualification.
It has been suggested that this resolution should go to the banking and commerce committee. If there were any possibility of varying the terms of the agreement, that might be worth while; but when it is a simple decision, whether Canada will or will not be a party to the agreement, it seems to me the question is sufficiently clear to make unnecessary any reference to a committee.
Questions have been asked about the details of the agreement. The agreement requires no great comment. The price fixed is the price between countries. It does not interfere with the policy of any country regarding its domestic wheat. We know that the United States intends to fix wheat prices for the current year somewhat above the maximum price provided for in the agreement for wheat sold to any export markets. Any country can do the same. I think that covers the situation.

speechtext: Yes. This resolution is with respect to two brief amendments to the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act to enable the dependents of personnel killed to obtain pensions as was intended in the original act; owing to certain circumstances, it has not been possible under the act for them to obtain those pensions. maintopic: WAR PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES

speechtext:
No difficulty has been experienced in that regard. Perhaps I might give a little more detailed explanation at this stage.
The effect of the bill to be introduced is to remove the time limit for application for pension in respect of a deceased Canadian merchant seaman and salt-water fisherman. It seems unreasonable to deny pension to dependents, who are otherwise entitled to it, simply because through ignorance of the statutory rights or
fMr. MeCubbin.]
other reasons, they did not comply with the statutory limit of twelve months. That applies to dependents. There are some cases in which they did not know that they were eligible; consequently the date will be extended. The bill should conform to the war pensions act on which it is based. In view of the limitation in section 7, the removal of the time limit in respect of death only will affect a comparatively small number of cases, but will permit of an award in certain instances of hardship. That is the first one.
The other portion of it deals with dependents of deceased members of the R.AJF. transport command. As hon. members will recall, it was necessary for necessitous circumstances to exist for them to be eligible. This amendment is to cover cases where necessitous circumstances may not have been in existence earlier, but now are.

maintopic: WAR PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES
subtopic: REMOVAL OF TIME LIMIT IN APPLICATION FOR CERTAIN PENSIONS
speechtext: Is the time limit to be removed entirely in connection with the dependents of merchant seamen and ferry command men, or is it simply to be extended?

maintopic: WAR PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES
subtopic: REMOVAL OF TIME LIMIT IN APPLICATION FOR CERTAIN PENSIONS
speechtext: It is a matter of removal, rather than extension, as applied to the dependents.

maintopic: WAR PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES
subtopic: REMOVAL OF TIME LIMIT IN APPLICATION FOR CERTAIN PENSIONS
speechtext: And also in respect to men in the ferry command?

maintopic: WAR PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES
subtopic: REMOVAL OF TIME LIMIT IN APPLICATION FOR CERTAIN PENSIONS
speechtext: That is right, for dependents.

maintopic: WAR PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES
subtopic: REMOVAL OF TIME LIMIT IN APPLICATION FOR CERTAIN PENSIONS
speechtext: I suggest to the minister that in all fairness the time limit against merchant seamen themselves should also be removed. Merchant seamen must apply within one year of suffering disability; otherwise they cannot obtain any pension. I suggest that is unfair. There should be no time limit against them, any more than against the dependents of a man who lost his life. It is difficult enough, goodness knows, for either a merchant seaman or his dependents to establish the right to pension, because the disability or death must have been caused directly by enemy action. I do suggest that there is no reason why there should be a time limit against merchant seamen themselves.

maintopic: WAR PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES
subtopic: REMOVAL OF TIME LIMIT IN APPLICATION FOR CERTAIN PENSIONS
speechtext: In the discussion which took place on this general subject there were no indications that any were suffering hardship because of the time limit. However I shall undertake to follow up the matter in the coming months, and if there should be such cases they will be taken into consideration.

maintopic: WAR PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES
subtopic: REMOVAL OF TIME LIMIT IN APPLICATION FOR CERTAIN PENSIONS
speechtext:
Is there any reason why there should be a time limit of one year or any other period of time against merchant seamen? There is no time limit for members of the army, the navy or the air force; they need

Civilian War Pensions and Allowances
only show that the disability was caused by war service. In those circumstances they can qualify for pension. Is there any reason why the same rule should not apply to members of the merchant navy, particularly in view of the fact that it is so much more difficult for them to establish the right to pension?

maintopic: WAR PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES
subtopic: REMOVAL OF TIME LIMIT IN APPLICATION FOR CERTAIN PENSIONS
speechtext: I should not like to answer the hon. member without looking more deeply into the matter. Like the hon. member, at the moment I cannot see any reason. However I should like to look into the background, and into the discussion concerning this matter, before I reply.

maintopic: WAR PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES
subtopic: REMOVAL OF TIME LIMIT IN APPLICATION FOR CERTAIN PENSIONS
speechtext:
I take it there will be some time between the passing of this resolution and the debate on the bill. Perhaps in that time the minister could give consideration to my suggestion. As he knows, once an act is amended it is difficult to have another amendment in the next year. The tendency is to delay, and the act may not be amended again for several, years.
Here is an amendment which should be brought in, in the same bill which amends the right of the dependents. I would urge that the minister give consideration to extending his amendment so that it would cover the merchant seaman himself, as well as the dependents of those who lost their lives.

maintopic: WAR PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES
subtopic: REMOVAL OF TIME LIMIT IN APPLICATION FOR CERTAIN PENSIONS
speechtext: While I have no knowledge rf any hardship being experienced with respect to the time limit for the men themselves, I do know of a number of cases of serious hardships which this bill will seek to correct. I would prefer at this stage, therefore, that these amendments now before us might be passed, and that the other matters might be given close attention.

maintopic: WAR PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES
subtopic: REMOVAL OF TIME LIMIT IN APPLICATION FOR CERTAIN PENSIONS
speechtext:
One reason the minister has not seen the effect of such cases is that the restrictions against merchant seamen, and for that matter against the dependents, are so very strict. It must be shown that the disability arose directly from enemy action. According to the figures given on June 15 to the committee on veterans affairs, there are only sixty-six merchant seamen drawing disability pension at the present time, although there were about 18,000 who served. There have been 490 favourable decisions for dependents of merchant seamen. Those figures show what a ridiculously small percentage of these people qualify for pension. As the minister knows, the merchant navy suffered a higher percentage of casualties, speaking relatively, than either the navy, the army or the air force. These men have not had a fair deal. Perhaps that is one reason why now
there are no further applications being made for pensions-simply because they were shut out one year after they suffered disability.
As the minister knows, that is an unfair situation. Men who went out from our ports -from Halifax or from Vancouver-and who were disabled, could not qualify for pension unless disability resulted directly from enemy action. For instance, I know of one man who stumbled during a black-out in England. He fell over the edge of his ship, and was killed. His dependents could not qualify because the death was not directly caused by enemy action. Another young lad went out from Vancouver and contracted a tropical disease, with the result that his health was ruined. He can get no pension because the disease could not be traced directly to enemy action.
Surely that is unfair. Not only should the time limit be removed for the men themselves, but the basis upon which pension is granted should be broadened. It is much too restricted now, when it states that a man must have suffered disability or that death must have been caused by direct enemy action. That portion of the act should be changed. I am sorry this is not being done in this amendment. This is a basic injustice which should be remedied, and now is the time to do so.

If the government of Canada feels that any man who served in the merchant marine is entitled to compensation for injuries he may have received while serving during the war, I am sure that this country will be ready to grant such compensation. maintopic: FLOOD CONDITIONS-BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaiker, before you leave the chair I should like to say a few words in connection with the floods in British Columbia. I shall not

Floods in British Columbia
go into details as to why the floods occurred or as to what might have been done to prevent them. My personal friend and colleague the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair), speaking on my behalf, made an excellent speech in that connection. I should like to express my appreciation to the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), who protected me during my absence in the way of a pair.
On behalf of my riding in particular and all the people affected by the flood, I wish to express our appreciation to all the people of Canada for the way in which they came to our assistance in what has become a national calamity. To the members of the armed forces and to everyone who has contributed in any way to our assistance, we express our appreciation.
I should like to mention one or two things on which the government should take action immediately. The government should immediately put a ceiling on hay and other feed. Already in British Columbia we have people going around trying to secure what feed will be available for next year and all available feed now for cattle. If the government has not already done so, it should immediately put a ceiling on all feed stuff for cattle in Canada.
I do not think the government has gone far enough in its concessions respecting income tax. I understand that the government has generously extended to the end of June the period during which farmers whose land is now ten to thirty feet under water may file their returns. The government could very well afford to wipe out income tax entirely for farmers in any of the flooded areas. I strongly urge that that action be taken by the government immediately.
I would also ask the government, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) makes his announcement, which I hope will not be later than tomorrow, to state what the eventual financial set-up is to be for the rehabilitation of our farmers. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver North it would have a great effect on the morale of the flood victims if they could know exactly where they stand and what is to be done in their behalf. I realize that the details cannot be worked out overnight, but surely by this time the government should be in a position to say what the federal government will do for the victims in all parts of British Columbia who have been flooded out.
I had the privilege of taking the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) over certain portions of my riding, and I was
very glad of that privilege because I know his sympathy with everybody in Canada and it must have affected him to see those flooded-out homes. I do not think we have ever had, in my time at least, a calamity which has affected the people of Canada so much as the recent floods in British Columbia. I for one shall make no attempt to estimate the damage. When you have from eight to thirty feet of water over your home or farm, how can even an engineer or other expert estimate the damage?
I am particularly interested to see that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) is listening to me, because I have been trying to catch his ear in this connection ever since 1940. I am not a diking expert, but I heard
20,000	of them tell me what ought to have been done in my riding, and I honestly believe that if governments of the past had done their duty we would have had no flood, at least in the immediate district in which I live.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) and I have consistently endeavoured to have the Department of Public Works secure adequate dredging equipment for the great Fraser river, which is one of the largest rivers on the North American continent. The only dredge we have available to keep that channel clear is a forty-year-old dredge which is constantly busy at the mouth of the river. I remember, as a boy, that where large boats used to go up the river you can now throw a stone across. Last summer at Calamity Point near the mouth of Harrison river I got out in my gum-boots and waded half way across the Fraser river. It does not take any engineer to know that if the water of the Fraser river cannot get out to the Pacific you will have river bank erosion and disastrous floods. I do not think we would have suffered half the damage that was done this year if proper dredging equipment had been secured when it should have been secured. I want the Minister of Public Works to tell me what steps he has taken to secure adequate dredging and other heavy equipment to restore the dikes and repair the damage that was done. One of the dredges that was brought in to construct Sumas dikes came from Panama. If we are to save this fertile valley from floods next year construction on these dikes must be started immediately. We cannot wait for six or eight months. The necessary equipment should be ordered today.
I had the pleasure of showing the Secretary of State for External Affairs how high the water was on the telegraph poles along the great Canadian Pacific railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company have never paid five cents on the construction and maintenance of
Floods in British Columbia

dikes. There have been at least three wash-outs on their line. They cannot deny what pictures show, and I can assure hon. members that I took good care to take plenty of pictures showing the water in front of my own home and throughout that whole area. I have a letter here from the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and I am going to take time to read it. I would not feel so bitter about this if I had not seen neighbours, sixty-five and seventy-five years of age, with their entire investment flooded out, with pianos and everything else floating down the stream, all of which could have been prevented if governments over the past twenty-five years had had any initiative and had taken the proper action. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company have never done anything in western Canada that they were not paid plenty for doing. They have refused to accept their responsibility. Either the president of the Canadian Pacific and his officials were deliberately giving false information to the minister, or he has otherwise been misinformed.
This is a letter sent to me by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) under date of November 3, quoting the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company:
The Mission subdivision extends from the main line at Mission, B.C., southerly for a distance of 10-1 miles to Huntingdon. It was placed in operation in June, 1891, that is, prior to the construction of the Matsqui dike. The company, from time to time, has been requested to contribute toward the cost of the Matsqui dike, but has consistently refused on the ground that the dike does not benefit the lands of the railway company. Under the Drainage, Diking and Development Act of British Columbia, provision is made for the exclusion from a diking district lands not benefited. In 1895, a court of revision, 'because the company's land did not benefit, exempted the company from assessments in connection with the dike.
That information was supplied to me in a letter dated November 3, 1947, and was given to the minister by the president of the company. I shall be glad to give pictures to the minister showing that the company put a dam across by rock filling near the Mission bridge, and did it for years. I asked a question whether rock had been dumped, and the answer I received in an order for return was that the department had no authority and no information. I, as a private member, was told that if I wanted this information I would have to ask the company for it.
The story is a little different this year. I have pictures which were taken in 1938 by a professional photographer, showing the rock being dumped in, rock which caused five feet of silt to flow over the British Columbia Telephone Company cables. They were not able

to raise the cable because of that silt. It also caused the bridge to go out two weeks ago, and took 100 feet of the Matsqui farmers' dike with it.
Apparently the government found out something different in the meantime, because on April 19, 1948, I received this letter from the Minister of Public Works telling me that they could now get this information, but that last year they did not know anybody with authority who could, and that I as a private member, last year, had better ask the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. This is the letter:
During the years 1937 to 194,5, the company has deposited approximately 44,OW tons of rock around' the piers of this bridge and soundings taken indicate that the dumping of this rock has raised the river bottom near the piers, but has scoured the channels between the piers so that the cross-section of the river at this point is approximately the same. Gauges placed above and below the bridge indicate that there has been n,o retarding of the flow due to the placing of the rock.
It was at this spot that a span of the famous Canadian Pacific railway bridge went out, taking with it a hundred feet of our dike. In 1894 or 1896 the Canadian Pacific Railway Company themselves drove the piles, some of which are still remaining, to protect this river bank. I shall be glad to produce these pictures for the minister.
I do not believe in recriminations. In May, 1948, I was not scoffed at exactly, but I do not think I received the entire approval of certain members of the government when I said that the two great trans-Canada railways would be out within twenty-four hours. Actually they were out within ten hours. I pointed out that it was not a Fraser valley matter; that it was a national matter. When you cut off the third city of the Dominion of Canada, which affects the economy of Canada, it must be a national matter. Recriminations will not get us anywhere.
It is up to the government of Canada to make known to the people of my riding and to the people of the Dominion of Canada what they intend to do. They should issue a definite statement now as to what they intend to do to rehabilitate, in so far as money can do so, these pioneers and these people who have lost their all.
What is to foe done for the municipalities?
I should like the government to state definitely, in conjunction with the provincial government, what is to be done. How are our municipal taxes to be met this year? Our schools must go on. I am speaking particularly of the Fraser valley because that is the place I know most about. Other hon. members can speak of the whole of British Columbia. I am

Floods in British Columbia
primarily interested in my own district and know more about it than I do of other districts. How are the municipalities to carry on their schools, how are they to re-establish their bridges, culverts and roads that have all been washed out, to say nothing at all of the personal loss of the individuals concerned? It is up to the Prime Minister to make a definite statement in that connection. He should tell us what action the federal government is going to take. He should make that statement tomorrow.
Perhaps I am a little overwrought. But when you have lived all your life in a district and you see such suffering among the people as I have seen, you are bound to get that way. Fortunately there has been no loss of human life. That is the most fortunate thing that came out of it. It is also fortunate that we have found out who our friends are. We found that the people of Vancouver, and the people of the entire province, responded to our call for help. Since that time, arrangements have been made, in part, by the two governments to recompense the people who have lost their all. I shall give one instance,- and it is typical of others. The Johnston Cartage Company of Vancouver sent their trucks and equipment out there, not knowing whether they would get them back or not, and knowing they would not be paid five cents. One of those trucks is under fifteen feet of water today. They did not ask whether they were to be paid or who was to replace the truck. The people of Vancouver sent equipment and other help at once.
I admit that the government has gone a long way so far in conjunction with the provincial government. What are they going to do to replace the dike? We in the Fraser valley will not be satisfied until we have the river controlled from top to bottom. We will not be satisfied unless we have a proper dike constructed, what we call a two-truck dike. You can stop any break in a dike if you are able to get at it with material and equipment. After all, we are a part of Canada. We demand that this dike be reconstructed, so that we can defend it, not only on behalf of the farmers of the Fraser valley but also on behalf of the entire people of Canada.
Two great trans-Canada railways have to be defended. The British Columbia Electric Railway Company have a railroad to Chilliwack which must be defended. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I am urging the government to give an immediate answer, indicating what is to be done by the federal government. I am urging the Minister of Public Works to tell us without further delay whether or not they are endeavouring to procure suitable dredging equipment,
so that such a catastrophe as this may never happen again in British Columbia or anywhere in the Dominion of Canada.

maintopic: FLOOD CONDITIONS-BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
First I should like to compliment the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) on his moving and able outline of the conditions in the Fraser valley. From the descriptions I have had of that area and from what I have seen of it, it is a major catastrophe. One of my friends told me that perhaps it will be the thing that will stand out in his memory as the greatest catastrophe that he has ever witnessed or will have to witness. The suffering is intense and the uncertainty of the people is terrific. They do not know whether to go to their lands and start all over again. Therefore I should like to support the hon. member in asking that rehabilitation measures be announced immediately in so far as replacement of equipment, crops and so on is concerned.
I should like to point out to the government that other areas as well have suffered loss. I have not mentioned my own area before, because of the outstanding difficulties of the Fraser valley. They were of first importance. Not so many people are affected on the Skeena river, but they have suffered just as intensely as the people of the Fraser valley. The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Matthews) has pointed out what happened in Kimberley and so on. Areas are affected all over the province. I wish the federal authority would step in and help flood victims wherever they are. It will be noticed how swiftly the United States federal authority steps into the picture when there is flood damage.
In my own area along the Skeena river, especially around the towns of Terrace and Usk there has been suffering. The province simply has not been measuring up to its responsibilities. I do not wish -to be too harsh. I think the thing is too big for them to handle. I know the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) has able and willing men in his department who could step in and assess difficulties and carry out the rehabilitation- measures that are necessary on the Skeena river.
I do not want to hold up the time of the house any longer because the question has been outlined before, but I thought it was about time that I brought in the Sk-eena so that the general picture could become apparent, and that an over-all flood policy would be brought into being by the federal authority and measures taken wherever there are flood victims.
Mr. HOWARD C. GREEN (Vancouver South): Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a vrord in support of the stand taken by the
Floods in British Columbia

hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruick-shank) and the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Archibald). I do not think it can be questioned that this is a national catastrophe. Certainly it is by far the worst situation the people of British Columbia have ever had to face, and we feel that the people of eastern Canada have been wonderful in the way in which they have given help at this time. The people of different cities, Montreal and Toronto, and many other centres, have helped out, and that very action has done more to create good will in British Columbia toward eastern Canada than anything else could have done.
Now, however, we are asking that the government make an announcement with regard to plans for rehabilitation. I believe it is necessary that the lead should come from here. The provincial government has been very good also in the way in which it has come to the rescue of those who have suffered so much, but there is need for the tw'o governments to get together and decide upon and announce some plans for the rehabilitation of these sufferers. We hope that an announcement will be made before the parliament prorogues. The need is great, and it will make all the difference to these people if an announcement is forthcoming before prorogation.
Mr. 0. L. JONES (Yale): Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on this matter; but, having flown over the area discussed, I am 100 per cent behind the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). I should like to point out, however, that other areas of British Columbia were flooded as well, and therefore, in dealing with this matter, it should be, not only relief for Fraser valley but relief for the whole of British Columbia. There are areas in Yale, such as Keremeos, Hedley and Grand Forks, that have suffered, though not on so vast a scale as the Fraser valley; but definitely, as individuals, men in those areas have suffered as greatly as individuals in the Fraser valley. I suggest, therefore, that any relief to be given should be given to all who suffered in British Columbia.
While this is an act of nature that could have been prevented to a certain extent, there is another danger to which I would call attention, and that is the level of Okanagan lake. This lake is now at least twelve inches higher than it has ever been before at this time of the year, and I would ask the Minister of Public Works whether it is his intention to implement the report that was made on the lake level and flood control about four or five years ago.

This was a splendid report. It covered controls of the Columbia river basin and the Okanagan valley, with all adjacent rivers and waters. If this report were implemented, the danger facing the towns of Penticton, Kelowna and all towns along Okanagan lake would be absent today. But it is greater than it ever was. Five years ago several buildings in Penticton were affected by water. Most of the cellars were full of water and many buildings could be reached only by boat. The condition in the next month will be equally grave, if not graver than it was at that time. In this case steps could have been taken and should have been taken to carry out the report made years ago by the engineers. Had that been done, there would be no danger today. I would ask the Minister of Public Works whether it is his intention to implement the report on flood control in the Okanagan valley in the immediate future.

Mr. DONALD M. FLEMING (Eglinton): Mr. Speaker, there are some events of recent days which I think call for some brief comment in this debate. They were given direct point by the fact that three new hon. members took their seats in the house today.
A statement was issued by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the ninth day of this month concerning the reasons for the defeat of government candidates in three byelections held this month. I do not propose to read the entire statement, but the first paragraph is as follows:
The lead which the C.C.F. has gained in the recent by-elections reflects the inevitable dislike felt by persons of all classes for high living costs, and privations and restrictions of any kind.
The statement concludes with this paragraph :
It is, however, the long run rather than the short run which counts for most. It would be a mistake to attach too much significance to C.C.F. gains in the present.
I am no alarmist, Mr. Speaker, and I do not think for one moment that the government defeats in these three by-elections, and the election of twenty-two C.C.F. members in the recent provincial election in Ontario, can be traced to the fact that all who voted for candidates of that party were socialists by any means. Far from it. They were prompted no doubt by unrest, and certainly by the failure of the government to grapple with the twin problems of high cost of living and high taxes. However, the result of the government's failure to grapple with these problems

Policies oj Political Parties
has been that the normal danger from socialism with its policies of regimentation and the peril it presents to our conception of individual freedom, is now accompanied by a further threat. Whether the C.C.F. like it or not-and they have indicated that they did not like it-the fact is that the C.C.F. candidates in those elections, both in Ontario and in the three federal by-elections, did receive the votes of the Labour-Progressive party in all except two provincial ridings in the city of Toronto. That is the fact.
The Labour-Progressive leader in Ontario has already been boasting of the fact that the C.C.F. candidates elected in the provincial election owe their election to communist support. I am not going to dwell on that theme, because I think the situation has been well known for some time, but I do wish to lay the responsibility where I think it belongs.
The responsibility for the apparent rise of the socialist threat in this country, with the assistance of communist support, I should like to trace back to the point where I think it properly begins. I think it began in February, 1942. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that in that month there were some federal byelections in this country. You will remember one of them well. There was another one held in the riding of York South, and for the first time a C.C.F. member was elected to the House of Commons from an Ontario riding because he received the full support of the Liberal machine in that by-election campaign. The Liberal party and the government kept a candidate out of the field in that by-election campaign.

speechtext:
Now it is out in public. May I point out to the hon. member that the remark made by Mr. McDowell at the Tory convention in Manitoba was made in the course of what appears to have been the main debate at that convention. If one reads about this convention in all three Winnipeg papers he will find that the main question was whether to stay in or get out of the Manitoba coalition. Those who argued on both sides had the same aim in view, namely, to take whichever course would be most likely to keep the C.C.F. out of power.
Other hon. members have already referred to the fusion candidates or the confusion candidates in Saskatchewan. There was drawn to my attention this morning an advertisement for the two non-C.C.F. candidates in the constituency of Saskatoon. Saskatoon is a two-member riding where there has been one of those saw-offs such as was referred to by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). The Tory leader, Mr. Ramsay, is a candidate there, and there is one Liberal candidate. There now appears in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix an advertisement for these two candidates, one Tory and one Liberal. The whole theme of the advertisement is that both of these candidates oppose socialism. Below the advertisement one reads two lines. First, this line:	.
This advertisement is inserted by a group of independent voters.
Then there is another line which says:
This^ advertisement is not inserted by the authority of either the Liberal or the Progressive Conservative party.
That is a symbol of the confusion that things have reached in Saskatchewan, so far as both old parties are concerned.
The hon. member for Eglinton who raised this matter this afternoon made it pretty clear that his chief concern was not with the question of why the Liberal party was losing ground, as set out by certain members opposite to their leader; his chief concern was why both the old parties are losing ground, including his own.
I have before me a table which I am not going to ask the house to put on the record, because it is not up to date anyway, having to

Policies oj Political Parties
do with federal by-elections that have taken place since 1945. This table was made up after the by-election in Yale, and does not include the figures for the by-elections in Ontario and Vancouver Centre. Up to that time there had been eight federal by-elections since the general election of 1945. This table, which I say I shall not take the time to read, gives the total votes that each of the three main parties, Liberal, Progressive Conservative and C.C.F. had in these ridings in 1945. Then it gives the votes that each of these parties had in the by-elections in these same ridings. When you add them all up you find that the Liberal vote dropped from 92,453 to 87,365, or a drop of 5-5 per cent. When you add up the vote of the Progressive Conservative candidates on the same basis you find that they had dropped from 62,134 to 51,937, or a drop of 16-4 per cent.. Therefore, when the hon. member for Eglinton talks about the disintegration of the Liberal party he cannot but be conscious of the even greater disintegration that is going on in his own party.
Contrast the decline in the total votes of the two old parties in these elections with the figures of the votes for the C.C.F. candidates. These include ridings like Pontiac where, as a matter of fact, we dropped. But when you add them all up-including Pontiac-you find that the C.C.F. went up from 27,218 votes to 43,216, or an increase of 58-7 per cent.
Let me repeat these percentages. The Liberal vote dropped 5-5 per cent; the Tory vote dropped 16-4 per cent, and the C.C.F. went up 58-7 per cent. That does not include Ontario and Vancouver Centre, which would make an even sorrier picture both for my hon. friends opposite and for the hon. member for Eglinton, who raised the question this afternoon, and an even better picture for the C.C.F.
What the hon. member for Eglinton and others of his party, who have spoken, do not [DOT] seem to realize is that the figures I have given of the progress being made by this movement indicate something far more than just a partisan political game. The hon. member for Eglinton, like his colleagues in Manitoba, thinks not in terms of policy, but rather in terms of politics, a case of trying to put the other rascals out so that they can get in.
What is actually happening in this country today is that the people have not forgotten the high hopes expressed during the war that this time, having won the war, we would also win the peace. The people of the country have not forgotten the idealism expressed by the Prime Minister when he indicated during the years of the war that we had to lay then the foundations for a better society after that struggle was over.
The people today want all the freedoms we have had in the past and more. They want those freedoms protected and enhanced in every possible way. They want, with all that, security and justice. They know that if there is not security, if there is not justice, freedom can be lost. The Canadian people think of security and justice and freedom not merely in abstract terms. They realize that security and justice and freedom mean good homes, steady employment, educational opportunities for the children of all, the best care that is possible of the people's health, over-all security against all the things that hit us over which we have no control, and dignified security in our old age.
The people of Canada do not see these things coming under the old, worn-out competitive free-enterprise system. The people of Canada have come to realize that social thinking has been moving away from the competitive dog-eat-dog method to the co-operative method, to the attempt to establish our lives on the basis of a community of human beings whose concern is to achieve, not big salaries for the few and the short end of the stick for the many, but a good life for all our people.
What my hon. friends do not seem to realize -and I do not blame them, because it is inevitable that in this political life we cannot but get into arguments back and forth-is that this conception is very deep in the hearts of the Canadian people, as expressed, Mr. Speaker, by the introduction this morning of three new C.C.F. members who walked up the aisle and were presented to Your Honour. They came to express the hopes, the desires and the determination of the Canadian people *that we turn our backs upon the old dog-eat-dog, cutthroat competition of the past and attempt to achieve the kind of society that we believe to be our destiny in this our Canada.

Perhaps he was to be pardoned for that, because it does lend itself to that. I suggest that this division among my Liberal friends opposite, which has been widely publicized, is serious and is something that calls for some statement to this house and to the country before parliament prorogues.
The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sin-nott) has written a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), and we have seen six members opposite, led by the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Breithaupt) calling upon the Prime Minister and insisting that the government come out of the kitchen, insisting that there should be a removal of austerity taxes on electrical and other household equipment, dropping the sales tax from any foods or commodities on which it still remains, and the use of subsidies again to bring down the high cost of basic food necessities. In addition to that, there is this quotation from the hon. member for Waterloo North:
Mr. King told us he believed our proposals were very wise.
At another place in the account of that interesting interview, the hon. member for Waterloo North is reported as having said:
Mr. King agreed with us that a housewives' budget would be very much in order.
The other day I asked the Minister of Finance whether it was the intention of the government to take any action to curb the still rising cost of living, and he told me in reply that he had nothing to add to what had been said on former occasions. He indulged in the usual attempt to tie price control and wage control together, and he left the whole thing on a very unsatisfactory basis. In the meantime there has been this wide publicity of a sharp division within the ranks of the party opposite. It is more than that. It sounds like a division between the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, because the Prime Minister is reported as having agreed with these six or seven rebel Liberals who want a different policy from that pursued by the Minister of Finance.
With the cost of living still going up, and prices of foodstuffs and the necessities of life still rising-another one was called to my attention a few days ago, namely the price of

textbooks, which will be from 50 to 75 per cent higher by the time the schools open in the fall than they are now-with this sort of thing happening, I suggest that this division in the party opposite is not just something to be trifled with from this side of the house; it is not just something to poke fun at. It is something that lays a responsibility on the government. It lays upon us the responsibility of asking the government for a statement as to which line it intends to follow. Does it intend to follow the line of austerity taxes and no consideration of subsidies, as pursued by the Minister of Finance, or the line of a housewife's budget and the use of subsidies to bring down the cost of living, as proposed by the hon. member for Waterloo North and five or six of his colleagues, and as agreed to, according to the newspaper reports, by the Prime Minister.
These things are of a somewhat different character from the line I was following a few moments ago. I was talking about a long-range idea, coming out of the heart of the Canadian people, as expressed by the C.C.F. victories recently. That trend will continue. There is no doubt about that. This other thing is immediate. The question is more important than whether it involves the disintegration of the Liberal party. It is a life-andi-death matter to the Canadian people now, whether the cost of living will be allowed to soar still higher, or whether some action will be taken to deal with the situation before it is too late. I hope that in this debate we shall have this question cleared up. If not, there should certainly be an answer before this session concludes.
