speechtext: Some one of the C.C.F. members has just said, "Well, they are doing pretty well". Yes, just a few at the top are doing well. But even they will find the situation rendered impossible for them if we continue under the present system, exactly in the way in which the Liberals are administering it, and exactly as the Progressive Conservatives would administer it if they were in power over on the treasury benches instead of sitting in opposition.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: Which they never will be.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not know
whether they will be, because you never can account for what the people will do.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: They may even vote C.C.F. now and again.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext:
There is an alternative.
I was telling the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) just before six o'clock that if the principle of the creation of debt-free money, in accordance with the production of the country, were adopted, that would be the key to a solution of the difficulty. I lay this down right now, that if that principle is not adopted by the Liberal party or by the Progressive Conservative party, or whatever party succeeds them, then the country will go toward a socialist dictatorship, just as sure as Canada is Canada. And so will any other country that tries to carry on under the system under which we are now carrying on.
If debt-free money is adopted we shall find that it will then be possible to render financially possible what is physically possible. All a country like Canada needs is to have what is physically possible, in this majestic and marvellous country, rendered financially possible. Then everyone of the fondest dreams of the people of Canada can be realized, because we can use the resources God has given us to accomplish a standard of living such as we ought to have.
I have already told what the C.C.F. stands for. Let me now say that social credit fundamentally stands for the use of debt-free money in accordance with the surplus production of the country, the production which, under normal circumstances, people are unable to obtain the money to buy. If the C.C.F. would adopt that principle, as I suspect a number of them would, they would be able to avoid-

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: The only kind of money they will ever have.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: There is no use in mincing matters. I want to be frank; if the C.C.F. did adopt the principle of debt-free money, then they would not be under the necessity of stealing every bit of money they use from the people who have it.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: Shame.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext:
All they are advocating at the present time is nothing in the world but organized highway robbery. They propose to take from the men who have, the money that they have. That proposal will discourage initiative; it will discourage people from producing. That is the difficulty the socialists run into all the time; they get to the point where they cannot get production and then they are in real difficulty.
If the C.C.F. will adopt the principle of debt-free money they will not have to have government ownership of industry, because they will be able to get their money without trying to take it way from those who have it. If the Liberals and Conservatives will adopt the principle of debt-free money, wisely used, they will be able to overcome the dangers they are running into. I have not much more to say and I am sure all will be glad to have me finish.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: No; it is a good speech.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: Give the C.C.F. another belt.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: Go after the Liberals again.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: I think I have been going after the Liberals just about as hard as I have been going after anybody. When we rose for the dinner recess I was pointing out the strange ways of the Liberals. One member of our Social Credit group stated in this house one time that a certain man with great experience in Canada had once said that the Liberals were false to true principles while the Conservatives were true to false principles.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext:
The C.C.F.
have no principles.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: Just the truth.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext:
I believe the C.C.F. are true to the principles they have, but those principles are false and will lead them into trouble. I was just pointing out what the Liberals have done with respect to debt-free money. The Liberal Advocate is supposed to be a Liberal party organ, or at least that is what it pretends to be. If you go back to the
Policies oj Political Parties

issues of that publication, from 1930 to 1935 you will find that in every single issue they talked about debt-free money. But just the minute the Liberals took office they stopped talking about debt-free money and they stopped all Liberals from talking about debt-free money.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext:
What about Gerry
McGeer?
Mr. QUE'LOH: They made him a senator.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: One of the most striking memories I have is of Gerry McGeer standing up in this house while the war was on and telling the then Minister of Finance, now the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley), how to conduct the affairs of this country with respect to money. I can remember the present Minister of Justice standing up and wringing his hands and pleading with the hon. member to stop embarrassing the government-by advocating principles which Liberals had been advocating for ten or fifteen years!

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: What did they do to Tucker?

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Tucker started talking debt-free money enthusiastically, and he persisted in such talk. I remember how earnestly he used to do so. What did the Liberals do with him? They sent him to the Bretton Woods conference.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: It was hard to take.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext:
What did they send him there for? I presume it was done in order to give an air of respectability to the Bretton Woods conference or to try to make people think that, because the Canadian government sent a 'monetary reformer to the Bretton Woods conference, the Bretton Woods conference stood for monetary reform. You could not have a bigger lie put out anywhere than that, for the Bretton Woods conference stood for everything but monetary reform; it stood for reaction, the gold standard and restriction in every direction.
What did they do with the former member for Rosthern, Mr. Tucker? When he came back here they made him parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, and that was the end of Walter Tucker. We heard no more from him regarding monetary reform. I could go right on through the list and refer to member after member. You rarely heard a man on the Liberal side rise in his place and talk in favour of monetary reform. Why? They were told, I suppose, to lay off. You can hardly get anywhere with a party that does things like that.

Oh, yes, the Liberals advocate these things like debt-free money in order to get into power, but they desert and betray them as soon as they get in. The Conservatives have not had courage enough to stand up and talk in favour of monetary reform.
What they need in the two parties are new ideas. The ordinary person on the street knows that some new ideas have to be brought in. but he does not know where in the world to turn to for them. So he votes for the C.C.F. because he thinks he can understand them a little better than he can understand anybody else. As I said a few minutes ago, it is easy for anybody to understand highway robbery. Even back in the days of Adam they understood that two or three could gang up on somebody who had some goods and take them away from him. That is all the C.C.F. are advocating. You hear them everlastingly talking about profits, but you never hear them say a word about losses. They pick out a few companies that happen to be fortunate enough in a given year to make profits, and they cry out against those profits as though the making of profit was the greatest crime of today. But they never tell you about the scores of others that made losses; they never tell you what the C.C.F. government would do to help them out.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext:
We do not have any
losses.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: You do not have any losses because somebody else is running the businesses. Just as soon as you run them yourselves you will have nothing but losses. That is precisely the sort of thing that socialism runs into.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: Wait until Thursday.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext:
C.C.F. people think everything will be fine just as soon as they are voted in. They are in that respect just like the Liberals and the Conservatives. The Liberals think that, because they win an election, they must be perfect. If the C.CJL also get the idea that, because they win an election, they must be all right, they are going to run into some terrible disappointments.
The members of the C.C.F. are well-meaning; every single member that is in this house means well. He is just as fine a man as you could possibly meet, but there is not a member of the C.C.F. in this house who has the slightest idea of what it would cost to put into operation the ideas he advocates.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: He does not know.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext:
Oh, yes, we do, right to the last cent.

Policies oj Political Parties

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: What a terrific shock the C.C.F. will run into if they take over the government and discover that there is limit to the amount of money that can be either taxed or robbed from the people of Canada. After they get all the money that can be taxed or robbed from the people, they will find they are far short of having enough money to run the affairs of Canada as they now tell the people they could run them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: The only limit is what is physically possible.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext:
Somebody has been talking about the social credit "printing presses". No one has ever heard anyone in the Social Credit group speak about printing presses, but you find that talk about printing presses taking place among Liberals, who are always trying to delude the people with falsehoods. How can you hope to run the country successfully when members of parliament are that kind of people? You just cannot do it. The people are becoming completely sick of the whole thing, but they do not know what to do.
Almost every country in the world, including Canada, is faced with two alternatives. Either they will have to adopt a system similar to social credit, which is based fundamentally upon the principle of debt-free money to render what is physically possible financially possible, or they will have to adopt socialism. There is no middle way. If they adopt socialism they will ultimately run into the same thing they have in Russia. That is inevitable. You may scoff at it all you like, but you cannot scoff the truth of my statement out of my statement.
This country faces those two alternatives. Either it will adopt the social credit concept, or it will adopt the C.C.F. socialist concept, and the two are diametrically opposite.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext:
Somebody says, "No", out I tell him that I know just about two things about it for every one he knows. I think I knew as much about socialism as the ordinary socialist in this house when I was twenty-five years old. I knew it then and I know it now. I used to wonder whether socialism was acceptable as a way of life, but I never was able to convince myself that it would lead to a sound state, and I do not believe it will now; not because I have any prejudices against it, but because the principles it advocates are unsound if you want freedom.
Just a word about enterprise. Social Credit stands for individual enterprise, for it says
that individual enterprise will produce goods abundantly. It has proved that it will do so all down through the centuries. At no time was the proof more evident than during the recent war when the nations that were under individual enterprise were able to smother with their production the nations not under free enterprise. I prefer to say "individual enterprise" rather than "free enterprise", because free enterprise suggests that enterprise is free to do whatever it likes, create monopolies and charge what it likes. Social Credit does not favour that sort of thing at all. Social Credit says that if you take individual enterprise, with the wonderful motivation that is in it naturally, set it to work producing goods, and regulate that enterprise by the social credit just price system, which allows for a fair profit, allows enterprise to recover its costs plus a fair profit, you will have a powerful engine, harnessed and controlled as a powerful horse might be, so that it can go ahead and produce abundantly without being able to destroy itself or others. There you have the concept of social credit.
We find our C.C.F. brethren very fond of trying to smear social credit in Alberta by trying to make it appear that social credit stands for big business, monopolies, et cetera.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: Where is Mr. Low?

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: He is in Saskatchewan trying to tell the people of Saskatchewan some of the truth.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: I have been trying to grasp the principles of social credit. My understanding is that it is controlled free enterprise. Is that correct?

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: I think you could say "controlled" or "regulated". It is difficult to get a word which will carry the exact truth without an unfortunate connotation.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: If it is controlled, how can it be free?

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext:
It can be free just as a man who has been taught good manners and who exercises a certain amount of restraint can move about freely without offending anybody. He does not lose his freedom through such restraint. Just as soon as individual enterprise is taught that the state will co-operate with a company-let us take the Aluminum Company of Canada or the Canadian Pacific as an example-just as soon as the Canadian Pacific would be assured that the people of Canada would co-operate with it in an endeavour to see that it could recover its costs of production, plus a fair profit, and that the people of Canada would be behind it

right through to accomplish that objective, the Canadian Pacific would become in every respect, one of the finest and most efficiently managed services in the state.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: It will be the government then.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext:
That is just nonsense -no attempt to get the truth! What I have said holds. Just as soon as the Canadian Pacific would be assured that it could recover its cost of production, plus a fair profit, and it knew what that profit would be, and everybody knew it; once it was assured that the government and the people would co-operate with it, the Canadian Pacific would have no further, anxiety. It would not have to be afraid that, in case of a slump or a depression, it would lose so much money that it would become impossible for the company to keep on running the road. The same holds true of any enterprise you may take in this country. The Canadian Pacific would be regulated or controlled, not only to prevent it from going too far but to keep it from falling too far short of its objectives.
Now you have the social credit concept of individual enterprise just as clearly as it can be briefly defined, and you know what social credit stands for as regards enterprise. It stands for a carefully regulated price structure which prevents any enterprise from exploiting either the people it serves or employs or buys its raw material from. We say that if you put individual enterprise in a set of circumstances like that it will produce in adequate abundance, and all you will need to do then will be to find a market for what it produces. Social credit says: We will find a market for your goods through the use of debt-free money.
You see how vastly different that is from socialist concept.
I say once more to the Liberals and the Conservatives that if they adopt that debt-free money principle, if they set out with it to build a policy which will commend itself to the people; they can put that policy at an early date into operation. And, once the policy is put into operation, the people will never listen to socialism or the C.C.F. any more, and communism will disappear.
I say once more, Mr. Speaker, that Canada shall have either social credit or socialism. We may just as well recognize that and govern ourselves accordingly.

they will learn to appreciate being members of this club, the House of Commons. I wish them success. I am not panicky at all about their election. It was due to entirely different causes from those enumerated by the speakers of that party this afternoon.
I have just listened with great pleasure to the entertaining speech of my hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore). He told us that this country will go socialist or social credit. If the country ever goes socialist, which God forbid, we shall know where we are going, but if the country ever goes social credit, we shall never know.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: Just as we do not know under Liberalism.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: I have listened attentively to my hon. friend, whom I admire. He tells us of the marvels that will be accomplished by social credit, but he failed to do one thing. maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.

speechtext: These are things that my hon. friend has said a number of times, and each time I could not understand the working of it. maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: The Liberal machine.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

These are things beyond my understanding. I listened with great care

The machine that can do that must be pretty good, but I do not know if it is invented yet.

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit another question? Will he tell us what Liberalism is?

maintopic: RECENT BY-ELECTIONS-SUGGESTED TAX CHANGES, COST OP LIVING, ETC.
speechtext: I will tell him what Liberalism is. Liberalism is the thing that my hon. friend believes in. When he makes sensible speeches they are Liberal speeches. When he denounces the socialist party he speaks as a great Liberal. It is unfortunate that he does not do so all the time.

I will tell the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Young) that if he was elected it was mostly for two reasons: in the first place, because the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) did not create that vacancy when I asked for it.

speechtext: Why did you ask for it?

speechtext:
For the reasons that my hon. friend used in the campaign. In the second place, because he complained that the official Liberal candidate had been imposed on the people of Vancouver Centre against their will. Parties may make mistakes at times, and when we make mistakes we admit them. This is no discredit to the hon. gentleman who, because he seems to be genial, must be personally popular in spite of the fact that he may have preached-I am not sure of it-wrong doctrines during the campaign. He preached wrong doctrines if he preached the C.C.F. doctrines.
I listened to the hon. member for Winnipeg: North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He said that the people thought of security, justice and freedom not merely in abstract terms. That is true. He said that the people of Canada- this may not be textually accurate, but I was careful in taking my notes, and I want to do him justice-generally wished good homes, steady employment, educational opportunities, more of public health and over-all security than that given under the old, worn-out competitive free enterprise system. That is his view. That is the socialist view which is in conformity with the teachings of the late Mr. Woodsworth. On the other hand, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre this afternoon said that the policies pursued by the two old parties led to authoritarianism, the possession of economic power by the few and the abolition of private property in the hands of the people. How can both statements be reconciled? It is impossible. If my hon. friend thinks private enterprise is wrong I do not see how the new member for Vancouver Centre can make himself the advocate of the right of ownership by the private individual.

Mr. Speaker, listening to the new hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Williams), one would think some of the things mentioned by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) were not worthwhile. Among the things he mentioned were old age pensions without a means test, income tax relief for those in the lower income brackets, the repeal of the 25 per cent excise tax on certain goods manufactured in Canada, a reduction in the cost of living and so on. If those things are not important, I do not know what are.
I want to congratulate the hon. member for Eglinton upon bringing up these matters. This is one of the most important subjects we have discussed this session. It also gives us an idea as to where true Liberalism is. I think we in this house who are Liberals will have an opportunity to get up and express our views. If we belonged to the socialist party or were under a dictatorship we would not have that opportunity. I would refer hon. members to what happened recently in Manitoba when a certain member of that party got up and expressed his view and was immediately read out of the party.
I do not think enough people in this country realize what true Liberalism is. I do not think they realize what free enterprise is. If they had a taste of socialism and communism as they have in Russia, they would possibly think more about it. In this democratic way of life of ours we have an opportunity to express our opinions as we see them.
Under the private enterprise system we have seen Canada rise from eleventh place among the trading nations of the world, to fourth place. That has all been done under private enterprise. We have seen conditions in Canada improve greatly, so that today our industrial production is at the highest pitch of any in the whole world.
I was not born with a silver spoon in my mouth. In 1926 I had to haul all my provisions to the bush to cut pulpwood for which I was paid $1.85 a cord. In 1933 I milked cows and shipped milk for seventy-five cents a hundred pounds. I know something about budgets, because I was the reeve of a municipality for eight years. I took over the reins when things were not very good and I know what all this means.
We hear a great deal about the Labour government in England, how they have no troubles over there, how everything is nice and rosy. Today ten ships are tied up at the London docks loaded with Canadian produce which is rotting because of strikes and labour troubles in London. Every time any labour 5849-357
trouble crops up in this country, up pops a C.C.F. member with a cure-all for everything. Yet their socialist friends in Britain cannot solve their own labour troubles.
There is one thing I believe in, Mr. Speaker, and the people of the constituency I represent would consider me remiss in my duty if I did not say it. Under our democratic system in this country we are the servants of the people, and not their masters, and if we do not pattern our programs to the liking of the people, they can vote us out. But never let it be forgotten that under socialism and communism, once it is in office, that power of the vote which for years has been the sacred right of our people under our democratic system, will be lost forever.

speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister a question on item 54. What policy is being followed by the Department of External Affairs in repatriating Canadian citizens who have been trapped1 in territories which were annexed to the Soviet Union during and after world war II? I have several cases referred to me of Canadian citizens who today find themselves in territories controlled by the Soviet Union. When I took the matter up with the department the reply I received was that nothing could be done for these persons unless they themselves obtained exit visas from Soviet authorities. It seems to me that that is an unfair attitude to take. Could not our Canadian representative undertake to place a request before the Soviet government to return these people to Canada?
I have in mind one person, an elderly lady, whose husband, a Canadian soldier, was killed in the war. Her son is now endeavouring to bring her to Canada. Apparently the department seems to be helpless in aiding him in the problem of bringing her over. Personally, I am not satisfied with the answeT that all we can do is to say that we will help her, provided that she obtains an exit visa from the Soviet authorities. I think that is placing the onus on a person who is not in a position to bargain with a totalitarian government. Surely we as a government can make a request of the Soviet authorities that they return to Canada certain persons who are Canadian citizens. Following such request, we would know, of course, whether the Soviet authorities would
Supply-External Affairs

agree to allow these persons to leave the country. To leave this matter entirely to these helpless people is unfair.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: There are two categories of persons who may be considered as being in the position described by the hon. member, persons having dual nationality and persons with only Canadian nationality. As to persons with only Canadian nationality, under international law we do make requests. I cannot say we are very successful. We have been carrying on the negotiations for nearly three years now with respect to a young lady who, according to our contention, has only Canadian nationality, and we have not yet succeeded in obtaining an exit visa for her.
As to those who have dual nationality, in certain cases we have made representations, and the answer to us has been that the person is a national of the Soviet republic, where he or she happens to be, and it is a matter of Soviet domestic policy that will have to be decided by the Soviet authorities. There is not. much else that we can do about the matter.
With respect to a person, perhaps persons, who, we feel, is or are truly of Canadian nationality, we have considered bringing the matter before the united nations as a violation of fundamental human rights, and the matter is under consideration. We would certainly have done that even at an earlier date, had we not feared that it might be detrimental rather than beneficial to the person concerned. The situation is a difficult one.
I can assure the hon. member that we will [DOT]do everything possible to be of assistance to those who have Canadian nationality, even though they may have dual nationality, but any own experience in connection with cases that have been brought to my personal attention does not allow me to extend very much hope of getting the kind of treatment that we would expect from a government maintaining friendly relations with us.

I could not- give an estimate of the numbers of those having dual nationality. Very few have applied to us for assistance. If 
the hon. member knows of any case and wishes to bring it to our attention, I can assure him that we will lose no time in communicating it to our representative in Moscow, or Budapest or Belgrade or wherever the appropriate official may be located.
Mr. MaeINNIS: The minister referred to dual nationality. I want to see if I understand what constitutes dual nationality. Would a woman, a Soviet citizen, marrying a Canadian, be considered as having dual nationality?

She would have to comply with the requirements of our citizenship act to become a Canadian citizen; but she would probably, even after that, having become a Canadian citizen, be still considered under Russian law to be a Soviet citizen. That is what I meant by dual nationality. To give a concrete example, a person, bom in Canada of parents who are French nationals, is, under French law, a Frenchman, but under Canadian law he is a Canadian and has for international law purposes dual nationality.

I should like to make a few remarks on our representation abroad. I am not speaking from direct personal knowledge, but I have had an opportunity throughout the year to talk to representatives of prominent Canadian firms who have been in South American countries. Some have been all over South America. The people to whom I have talked I regard as responsible people not given to complaining in a petty way. They know what they are talking about. Therefore I think there must be some basis for their criticism of some of the representation abroad.
As to the South American countries, I have heard the criticism expressed that we have two types of representatives, namely, either older men who are past their days of usefulness or their days of activity-when those who have not passed that stage are so necessary at the present time adequately to represent any country-or we are represented by younger men who are graduates of universities and are without doubt men of ability but who, these people tell me, have not had sufficient training in diplomatic work.
With regard to South America, I was informed that the major criticisms were, first, that few of our representatives abroad actually spoke well the language of the country to which they were sent, and I should like the minister to comment on that; in the second place, that many of them, the younger men particularly, were academic in their approach to life and did not appear to have a sound understanding of business principles; and in the third place, that they were not experienced in the diplomatic service sufficiently to understand the ways of the country to which they were sent, the sensitivity of the people of other countries to certain practices and customs, and so on.
With reference to European countries, I heard this criticism expressed. People who, I think, are well informed, consider that some of our representatives are kept at their posts far beyond the age of usefulness.
With regard to the South American countries, I am informed that some of our representation is of such an order that South American firms are dealing directly with Canadian firms, not taking advantage of the trade services and not taking advantage of our Canadian diplomatic services. As I said before, I have no personal knowledge on these matters, but I should like the minister to
comment on my remarks and to explain to the committee the qualifications that are required for appointment to these positions, particularly the senior positions, and to say if it is the regulation that those representing Canada in a given country shall be able to>
speak well the language of the country to-which they are sent. That is a serious matter from the point of view of being able to represent this country anywhere abroad.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is difficult for me to make any comment on the observations the hon. member has made, because they are so contrary to the comments I receive from numerous travellers abroad who write to me to compliment the department on the effi-cicncv of the services performed by its representatives. If the hon. member would be kind enough to bring to my attention personally and confidentially-I know he would not wish to do it here publicly-the complaints he may have heard concerning these missions, I shall be obliged to him, and I think he will be rendering a service to the country. We are expanding quite rapidly; we are spending taxpayers' money on these representations abroad, and it is our keen desire to be as well represented abroad as possible.
It is probable that there are in some of these legations ambassadors or ministers who do not speak fluently the language of the country. In South America, Spanish is the language spoken in all the republics but Brazil. But in the capitals of all those South American republics, a large element of the population speaks French or English. It is a decided advantage to be represented by someone who acquires the facility to speak in the language of the country to which he is sent and even to make public addresses in that language. We know that from the glowing reports we receive, for instance, of the success of Mr. Jean Desy in Brazil. He took the trouble, and it did not take him long, to master the Portuguese language. The reports we have had sav that Mr. Desy had created in Brazil the impression that Canada was a modern Athens where practically the whole of the people were of the highest order of culture, both in letters, in the arts, and in music.
An amusing article was published in one of the United States magazines to the effect that we were taking some time in finding a successor to Mr. Desy, because we felt that it would be difficult to maintain the kind of impression about Canadians that he had created there. But Mr. Desy has been replaced by Mr. Scott Macdonald who had his training in perhaps the same spheres, but also in other spheres as well, and who speaks English and
Supply-External Affairs

French. He speaks some Spanish, but I do not know whether he speaks Portuguese. Nevertheless, the reports we get are that in the short time has has been there, he has also been making a good impression. I am saying *quite frankly to the hon. member that in general we get glowing reports of the efficiency of our representation; and if he has information about any one or more of these missions and will convey that information to me confidentially, I shall be grateful to him, because it is our desire to have the best possible representation.
The hon. member says we are suffering from the fact that we have some men who are beyond middle age and some who have not reached middle age. The hon. member will recognize that, as a consequence of the first great war, there was a gap in our population, and we are feeling that in many walks of life. I am proud to be able to say that the Department of External Affairs is attracting a high class of men from our institutions of learning. Some time ago we advertised for fifteen appointments as third secretaries. The educational standards required were high. Over 300 applicants took the examinations, so that for fifteen appointments we had 300 who had the academic qualifications, who wrote the examinations, and from whom we were privileged to select fifteen. I think we are getting into the service men who will be able to serve Canada with credit to themselves and advantage to the country. It takes some time to train them, and we have had the advantage of securing several well qualified public servants from other branches of the civil service. We are using our best endeavours to make our representation abroad truly' representative of Canada.

In looking over the
details, I was interested to note that the high commissioners come first and then follow the amounts for the various ambassadors abroad.
I understand that in the table of diplomatic precedence our high commissioners follow ambassadors and probably ministers. Would the minister explain why it is that the high commissioners do not take what I would call their rightful place according to seniority in the diplomatic ranks?
For instance, here in Canada we have the high commissioner for Eire, an able gentleman in the person of Mr. Hearne. If seniority were to count from the date of appointment he would probably be the doyen of the diplomatic corps. However, any ambassador from a foreign country now takes precedence over him, and the same thing must work in regard to the high commissioners representing Canada in the other countries of the commonwealth.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The tables of precedence are established by His Majesty. The high commissioners are not representatives of what we would term "foreign countries"; they are representatives of countries of the commonwealth and have not the rank of ambassadors. Ambassadors are accredited by the head of a state to the head of a state. Ambassadors or ministers in Canada are accredited to His Majesty the King by the heads of the states they represent. The way the constitution has developed, His Majesty the King would as King of England be accrediting a high commissioner to His Majesty as King of Canada. It is not done. The high commissioner represents the government of the United Kingdom and is accredited to the government of Canada, not to His Majesty the King.
I think that is an anomaly; it is a vestige of the way things have developed. It has been under discussion for some time with the various governments of the commonwealth, and I hope the time will come when it will be removed and when these representatives of the sister nations of the commonwealth
Supply-External Affairs

will have within the commonwealth the precedence that normally would be theirs if we were not all nations of the commonwealth. I do not think that would mean any loosening of commonwealth ties, and I hope some day it will be recognized in that light.

I was really pleased when I had occasion to meet a number of these men in our foreign service in Italy, France, Germany and the United Kingdom, and I have nothing but praise for them.
I think it is to the advantage of the country to have older men in the service along with the younger men. I do not think it would be wise for any country to appoint young men only to foreign service, because the older men who are in it have had many years of experience, particularly those who have served in a military capacity. be of great assistance to our younger men. Our young men have been learning very fast, and I was indeed pleased to find that they were doing excellent work in the various countries.
I should like to ask the minister why Canada limits her representation to the small number of representatives we have in the various countries? Canada has grown up to occupy an important position in the world, and in my opinion we have not a sufficient number of men in our foreign service. Surely we could train a number of our younger men who have seen service in the last war and then send them out into various countries. When we had ninety-nine, we had a clerical staff abroad of 315, and when we had 111, we had a clerical staff abroad of 493. When you increase your representation abroad, if you are to make the proper use of the reports and information gathered there, you have to make a proportionate increase in your staff in the head office. speechtext:
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw to your attention a matter which affects the rights and privileges of myself and of every member of the house. The Evening Citizen carries a report which says a highly placed informant has told the Canadian Press that the government has decided to withdraw the special 25 per cent excise tax imposed on a broad list of goods. If that report is true I suggest that not only is it a gross breach of the privilege of members of parliament, but it is in effect a gross budget leak, and it is also a monkey wrench thrown into the business of the country. The government should inform us in the morning as to what the truth is. I propose to raise the matter again when the house meets in the morning. And I would say that the report further makes the outrageous suggestion that the government is considering whether this should be removed by legislation or by order in council. In other words, this report is suggesting that the government is waiting until parliament is prorogued in order to do this by order in council.
I repeat that if this is true, then whoever was responsible should be dealt with in the most exemplary manner, and I wish further to say that I will raise this question again when the house reassembles tomorrow morning.
